## Tissue Loading Shift and True Shear at L4-L5: Textual Mapping

### Step 1: Geometric Condition Established

The previously isolated geometry—a convex-posterior lumbar arc with no lordotic inflection—corresponds to what the text identifies as the condition where "the lumbar spine becomes fully flexed (rounded forward)" (Page 3).

### Step 2: Muscle-to-Ligament Loading Shift

The text states, citing Dr. McGill's EMG studies:

> *"As the lumbar spine becomes fully flexed (rounded forward), the contribution of the muscles to the required torque decreases and the supportive force generated by the ligaments increases. So, in effect, you switch off your muscles and allow your ligaments to support the weight."* (Page 3)

This constitutes the critical tissue loading shift: the **spinal erector musculature** is deactivated, and the **interspinous ligaments** assume the torque-bearing role.

### Step 3: Consequence for Lines of Action

The text describes two distinct lines of action and their opposing effects on shear:

**Spinal Erector Musculature (now inactive):**
The text states that the spinal erector muscle force is *"predominantly parallel to the spine but also pulls back to counteract the forward shear"* (Page 3). When these muscles are active with a maintained lordosis, *"a component of this large muscle force will neutralize the shear produced by the load and body mass"* (Page 3). Under the observed flexed geometry, this protective posterior-directed shear component is **absent**, because the muscles have been electrically deactivated as confirmed by Dr. McGill's studies.

**Interspinous Ligaments (now load-bearing):**
The text specifies that *"the line of pull of the interspinous lumbar ligaments means they actually add to the shear component"* (Page 3). Figure 3 in the text is explicitly described as showing that *"the muscle force is absent and is therefore unable to help reduce the joint shear. Although the ligaments can counteract the load torque (allowing you to lift with a flexed back), the line of action of the ligament force adds to the joint shear"* (Page 3).

### Step 4: Effect on True Shear

The text defines true shear (termed "joint shear") as follows:

> *"The true shear on the L4-L5 joint (called the joint shear) is the resultant shear force produced by the sum of the reaction shear and the muscle/ligament shear."* (Page 2)

Under the observed geometry, this summation is mechanically altered in two compounding ways:

1. **Reaction shear remains present** — gravity continues to pull the load and upper body downward, producing a shear component across the L4-L5 joint surface. The text notes this force increases as the trunk approaches horizontal, which is consistent with the observed geometry.

2. **Muscle/ligament shear reverses direction** — in a lordotic spine, the muscle shear component *opposes* the reaction shear (reducing the resultant). In the observed flexed geometry, the ligament shear component now *adds to* the reaction shear rather than subtracting from it.

Therefore, the true joint shear at L4-L5 is no longer:

> Reaction Shear **minus** Muscle Shear Component

It becomes:

> Reaction Shear **plus** Ligament Shear Component

The text summarizes this combined effect: *"the joint shear...becomes very large indeed"* (Page 3). The quantitative output from the 4DWATBAK model confirms this: for a 300-pound load, joint shear escalates from **699 N** (normal lordosis, muscle-borne) to **3,799 N** (fully flexed, ligament-borne)—a factor of approximately **5.4×** (Page 5).

## Tissue Loading Shift and Its Effect on True Shear at L4-L5

### Step 1: Mapping Observed Geometry to the Text's Defined Condition

The geometry observed in Image B — a posteriorly-directed convex curvature of the lumbar spine with no visible lordotic segment — corresponds to what the text defines as a "fully flexed" lumbar spine (Page 3: "as the lumbar spine becomes fully flexed (rounded forward)").

### Step 2: The Loading Shift — Muscles to Ligaments

The text states, citing Dr. McGill's EMG studies:

> "Dr. McGill has shown conclusively with studies analyzing the electrical activity of the spinal erectors that as the lumbar spine becomes fully flexed (rounded forward), the contribution of the muscles to the required torque decreases and the supportive force generated by the ligaments increases. So, in effect, you switch off your muscles and allow your ligaments to support the weight." (Page 3)

Therefore, in the geometry observed in Image B, the **spinal erector musculature is deactivated** and the **interspinous ligaments** assume the role of generating the opposing torque to counterbalance the load.

### Step 3: How This Alters "True Shear" — Lines of Action

The text defines "true shear" (joint shear) as:

> "the resultant shear force produced by the sum of the reaction shear and the muscle/ligament shear" (Page 2)

**When muscles are active (normal lordosis):**
The text states the line of action of the spinal erector musculature is "predominantly parallel to the spine but also pulls back to counteract the forward shear" (Page 3). A component of the large muscle force therefore **reduces** the reaction shear. The muscle force acts to **neutralize** the shear produced by the load and body mass (Page 3: "the muscle forces offset the shearing effect of the weight (force) of the load and upper body").

**When ligaments bear the load (fully flexed spine — the observed geometry):**
Two compounding effects occur:

1. **Loss of shear-opposing muscle force:** "the muscle force is absent and is therefore unable to help reduce the joint shear" (Page 3). The component that previously counteracted forward shear is eliminated.

2. **Ligament line of action adds to shear:** The text explicitly states: "the line of pull of the interspinous lumbar ligaments means they actually add to the shear component" (Page 3). Figure 3's description confirms: "the line of action of the ligament force adds to the joint shear, which becomes very large indeed" (Page 3).

### Step 4: The Net Effect on True Shear

The "true shear" is therefore altered in two simultaneous ways:

- The **subtractive** muscle/ligament shear component (which previously opposed reaction shear) is **removed**.
- A new **additive** ligament shear component is **introduced**, acting in the **same direction** as the reaction shear.

The resultant joint shear becomes the reaction shear **plus** the ligament-generated shear, rather than the reaction shear **minus** the muscle-generated opposing shear. This transforms the true shear from a partially-neutralized value to a compounded, significantly elevated value.

The text quantifies this for a 300-lb load: correct form yields 699 N joint shear, while the fully flexed position yields 3,799 N — a difference attributable entirely to this reversal in the direction of the muscle/ligament shear contribution relative to the reaction shear (Page 5).

Whether the spine is in normal lordosis (muscles bearing the load, as in Video A) or fully flexed (ligaments bearing the load, as in Image B), the **torque that must be counteracted** is determined by the load weight and upper body mass acting at a distance from the L4-L5 joint center of rotation. **Contamination effect:** Without Pages 7–8 between Page 6 and Page 9, the Eagle Lite limitation appears to be a purely commercial restriction (like a trial-version limitation) rather than a physically meaningful boundary. This mischaracterizes the tool selection process from a physics-informed decision to a price-tier decision.

**Visible evidence that confirms misalignment:** Page 9's Altium section says "De-facto option for high-speed designs and complex PCBs." Without Page 8's via types and layer counts, "complex PCBs" is undefined — is it more components? More layers? Tighter spacing? The operator cannot evaluate this claim.

### RESULT 3: Suspension Area

**Suspended Page A: Page 2 ("About Me")**

**Why it cannot enter the main line:**
- The main line (Page 1 → 3 → 7 → 8 → 5) answers "What is it?" → "What is it made of?" → "Why does it matter?" Page 2 answers "Who is telling you this?" — a fundamentally different question type.
- Its role (credential-setting) serves the AUDIENCE's trust, not the OPERATOR's comprehension of PCBs. In the main line, roles are consistent: learner-becoming-designer. Page 2 briefly makes the learner an evaluator-of-authority, then never uses that evaluation again.
- Its prerequisite (Page 1 only) and its independence from structural knowledge mean it cannot be positioned between Pages 3 and 7 without interrupting the definitional chain.

**Why it should NOT be deleted:**
- Page 9 compares three EDA tools and states Eagle is "commonly used by makers." The author's background (CS graduate, not EE) from Page 2 explains WHY this presentation recommends Eagle over Altium: Eagle's XML/ASCII format is version-control friendly (a CS concern), while Altium's binary format is "terrible for version-control." Without Page 2, this tool recommendation appears arbitrary rather than discipline-grounded.
- Page 6 lists "Properly share your design with others" as an objective. Page 2's mention of GitHub (the URL: github.com/yeokm1/intro-to-pcb-design-eagle) is the only evidence that sharing means open-source version-controlled sharing, not just emailing files.

---

**Suspended Page B: Page 4 ("Before the PCB")**

**Why it cannot enter the main line:**
- The main line moves from definition → structure → structure-extension → constraints. Page 4 is a COMPARISON TEST (wire-wrapping vs. PCB), which validates rather than advances. Its function is proof, not progression.
- Its question type ("Can you see that this is better?") is observational/evaluative. The main line's questions are all constructive ("What is it? What layers? What constraints?"). Mixing validation with construction breaks the procedural flow.
- Inserting it between Pages 3 and 7 would mean: define PCB → prove PCB is good → describe PCB layers. The "prove" step interrupts the definition-to-specification gradient.

**Why it should NOT be deleted:**
- Page 5 claims "Reduce mistakes in manual wiring/soldering" as a motivation. Page 4's wire-wrapping photograph is the ONLY visual evidence of what "manual wiring mistakes" look like. Without Page 4, Page 5's claim is an unsupported assertion.
- The Novena laptop PCB image on Page 4 is the only example of a REAL PRODUCT PCB in the 10 pages. All other PCB images (Pages 1, 7, 8) are either the author's 555 Blinky project or diagrams. Deleting Page 4 removes the only industry-scale validation sample.

### RESULT 4: Adjacent Pages That Cannot Be Separated / Adjacent Pages That Cannot Be Combined

---

#### SET A: Adjacent Pages That CANNOT Be Separated — Pages 7 and 8

**Evidence of inseparability from the material:**

1. **Explicit back-reference:** Page 7 states "Usually 1.6mm thick." Page 8's title says "Structure of a (≥2) multi-layer PCB board" and the diagram shows "Total Height (1.834mm)." The thickness comparison only makes sense with Page 7's baseline immediately preceding. If another page (e.g., Page 9) is inserted between them, the reader must remember "1.6mm" from an interrupted context.

2. **Vocabulary dependency:** Page 8 says "2-layer board = 2 copper layers" — the term "copper layer" is defined in Page 7 as the layer that "Contains the traces (wires) between components" and "Also contains a ground/power plane." Without immediate adjacency, this definition fades and the arithmetic statement becomes opaque.

3. **Layer-counting logic:** Page 7 defines a 1-layer board with one copper layer. Page 8 immediately scales this: "2-layer board = 2 copper layers, 4-layer board = 4 copper layers, etc." This is a counting extension that requires the single-case to be fresh. The text even says "applies to 2-4 layers too" — the word "too" linguistically points backward to an immediate antecedent.

4. **Soldermask scope:** Page 7 defines soldermask. Page 8 refines: "Silkscreen and soldermask on top and bottom only." This restriction only makes sense if the operator just learned what soldermask is and can now ask "but where does it go on a multi-layer board?" Separation would break this question-answer pair.

**Separation test:** Insert Page 5 (Motivation) between Pages 7 and 8. The word "too" in Page 8's thickness note now points to a motivation page, not a thickness specification. The via types (Blind, Buried, Through-hole) arrive after a discussion of "Aesthetics" and "Durability" rather than after the copper/substrate model. The contamination is structural vocabulary being interrupted by constraint vocabulary.

---

#### SET B: Adjacent Pages That CANNOT Be Combined — Pages 4 and 5

**Despite being adjacent and topically aligned (both argue for PCBs over alternatives), they cannot be combined because:**

1. **Different question types:**
   - Page 4 asks: "Can you OBSERVE the difference between the old way and the new way?" (Visual comparison — a Test Well function)
   - Page 5 asks: "What CONSTRAINTS make the new way necessary?" (Abstract enumeration — a Manufacturing Regulations function)
   - Combining them would collapse a validation sample into a constraint list, eliminating the distinct observational function.

2. **Different roles served:**
   - Page 4 serves the **skeptic** who needs photographic evidence. The wire-wrapping photo and the Novena photo are EVIDENCE, not arguments.
   - Page 5 serves the **decision-maker** who needs an enumerated list of factors. "Space and weight constraints," "Making multiple copies," "Aesthetics," "Durability" are CRITERIA, not evidence.
   - A combined page would force the skeptic and the decision-maker to be the same person at the same moment, which contradicts the distinct rhetorical functions.

3. **Different prerequisites:**
   - Page 4 requires only Page 3 (know what a PCB is → now see why it's better than wire-wrapping).
   - Page 5 requires Pages 3 AND 4 (know what a PCB is + have seen the visual proof → now enumerate the formal reasons). The "Reduce mistakes in manual wiring/soldering" bullet on Page 5 implicitly relies on having SEEN the wire-wrapping mess of Page 4.
   - If combined, the prerequisite difference vanishes, and the constraint "reduce mistakes" appears without visual grounding — it becomes an assertion rather than a conclusion drawn from evidence.

4. **Different column memberships:**
   - Page 4 belongs to **Test Well** (validation/comparison)
   - Page 5 belongs to **Manufacturing Regulations** (constraints/rules)
   - Combining them would force one page to occupy two columns simultaneously, violating the lab bench structure.

**Combination test:** Merge into one page titled "Why PCBs? Evidence and Motivation." The wire-wrapping photo now sits next to the bullet "Aesthetics." Is aesthetics the reason PCBs are better than wire-wrapping? The photo suggests the reason is FUNCTIONALITY (reducing errors, enabling complexity), not aesthetics. The Novena PCB photo next to "Space and weight constraints" implies the Novena was designed for its small size — but the Novena is actually a full laptop motherboard, chosen for its COMPLEXITY, not its compactness. The visual evidence and the abstract constraints argue DIFFERENT things about PCBs, and forcing them into one frame creates false correspondences.

## Final Contamination Note for Subsequent Rounds

All future pages entering this lab bench must be checked against the following first-round contamination rules:

- **Principle Road** accepts only pages defining the PCB's physical/structural identity. Any page claiming structural content but primarily serving a different function (e.g., a page showing layer structure to sell a specific tool) is contaminated and must be rerouted to Wiring Lane or Rework Board.
- **Wiring Lane** accepts only pages about connection methodology (tools, interfaces, routing endpoints). A page listing components for a bill-of-materials purpose (purchasing, not routing) would be contaminated.
- **Manufacturing Regulations** accepts only pages naming constraints, rules, or production decisions. Motivation that doesn't translate to a design constraint is contaminated → Rework Board.
- **Test Well** accepts only pages providing observable comparison or measurable validation. Opinion without evidence is contaminated → Rework Board.
- **Rework Board** accepts framing, credentials, scope, and meta-commentary. Any page that advances substantive PCB knowledge is contaminated and must be rerouted to a content column.

### Box 4: Minimal revision

**Partial retention method:** Shared nouns/diagrams may be used as a PRELIMINARY SIGNAL that two pages MIGHT discuss related objects — but the signal must be tested against the three-criteria rule (same question type + same role/time + same prerequisites). The procedure is:

1. Observe shared noun/diagram → FLAG as potentially related
2. Check: Do both pages answer the same TYPE of question? (If no → different columns, stop)
3. Check: Do both pages serve the same role at the same time? (If no → different modes, stop)
4. Check: Do both pages require the same prerequisites? (If no → different registration points, stop)
5. Only if ALL THREE pass → pages may be considered "same object" candidates for combination

For Pages 7 and 8: Step 2 passes (both answer "What is it made of?"). Step 3 passes (both serve the learner at structural-understanding phase). Step 4 FAILS (Page 8 requires Page 7; Page 7 does not require Page 8). Conclusion: related but NOT combinable. They share a column but occupy sequential positions.

The noun/diagram match is retained as a SORTING HEURISTIC but not as a MERGING DECISION.

**Why this is enough to divert the main line:**

### CATEGORY 3: LATE PAGES — "Can only be taken out in the second half"

**Page 8 — "Structure of a (≥2) multi-layer PCB board"**

**Why late, not anchor:** Page 8 CANNOT be read first. Its opening statement — "2-layer board = 2 copper layers, 4-layer board = 4 copper layers, etc" — is a counting extension of Page 7's single copper layer. Without Page 7 preceding it, the arithmetic ("2 = 2, 4 = 4") references a base unit (one copper layer) never defined. The via types (Blind, Buried, Through-hole) describe HOLES between layers — but the reader must first know what a single layer's composition IS (Silkscreen, Soldermask, Copper, Substrate from Page 7) before understanding holes that connect those layers.

**Why late, not reinforcement:** Reinforcement pages make the main line "thinner" if missing but don't break anything. Page 8, if PLACED EARLY, actively BREAKS comprehension. The word "too" in "Usually 1.6mm thick – applies to 2-4 layers too" grammatically demands an antecedent. At the beginning, there's no antecedent — the "too" dangles, pointing at nothing. A reinforcement page merely thins; a late page actively damages if displaced forward.

**What breaks if placed early:** The boundary between "what is a layer" and "how many layers can you have" disappears. The reader cannot distinguish between learning a concept and scaling a concept because both arrive simultaneously. The Principle Road column's internal loading sequence (Page 7 loads → Page 8 concludes) collapses into a single undifferentiated structural dump.

**Specific indicator that this is a late page:** The diagram shows "Total Height (1.834mm)" with three via types numbered 1, 2, 3. Number 1 (Blind) is explicitly annotated "only for >2 layer board." This caveat only makes sense AFTER the reader knows what a 2-layer board is, which requires knowing what a 1-layer board is (Page 7), which requires knowing what a PCB is (Page 3). It's three prerequisites deep — definitionally late.

**Page 10 — "Component packages"**

**Why late, not anchor:** Page 10 lists physical dimensions: "0603 (0.063 inch × 0.031 inch), 0805 (0.079 in × 0.049 in)." These numbers describe SOLDER PADS on COPPER LAYERS — terms from Page 7. The phrase "Determines number of solder pads/sizes" assumes the reader knows what a solder pad is (Page 7 defines soldermask's function: "Prevent solder from flowing out of designated areas"). Without Page 7, pad dimensions are floating numbers without physical context.

**Why late, not reinforcement:** Reinforcement pages can be absent without damage. Page 10, if placed EARLY, creates a specific false impression: that PCB design begins with component selection. In reality (per the material's own structure), design begins with understanding the BOARD (Pages 3, 7, 8) and then selecting TOOLS (Page 9). Components are the LAST specification because they depend on both board structure (what pads can exist) and tool capability (what the EDA can route). Placing Page 10 early inverts the causal chain: objects → board, when it should be board → objects.

**What breaks if placed early:** The boundary between "what the board provides" and "what goes on the board" disappears. Page 10 lists ICs like "QFN-48 (Quad Flat No leads 48 pins)" — understanding this requires knowing that pads (not through-holes) will connect the QFN to the copper layer. Without Pages 7-8, the reader cannot distinguish between a QFN-48 (surface mount, needs pads) and a DIP-48 (through-hole, needs drilled holes). The package-selection decision becomes uninformed.

**Specific indicator:** Page 10's last section lists "Others: Ports like USB, audio, Board to board connectors like DF40C(2.0)-70DS-0.4V." The board-to-board connector implies at least TWO boards connecting — which implies understanding that each board has its own layer structure (Page 7), potentially multi-layer (Page 8). This inter-board connection concept is maximally late in the knowledge sequence.

### CATEGORY 4: PAIRING PAGES — "Looks key alone, but must be paired to be safe"

---

**Page 7 — "Structure of a 1-layer PCB board"**

**Why pairing, not anchor:** Page 7 LOOKS self-sufficient — its cross-section diagram labels four layers, provides a measurement (1.6mm), and defines each layer's function. A person encountering it alone might think: "I now understand PCB structure." But this is UNSAFE because:

- **Without Page 3 as partner:** The diagram shows WHAT a PCB is made of, but never states WHAT IT DOES. A reader could study the four layers and still not understand that the purpose is "to attach components to make a circuit." They'd know the materials without knowing the function.
- **Without Page 8 as partner:** The "1-layer" in the title implies this is the complete story. A reader encountering only Page 7 would incorrectly believe all PCBs have one copper layer. They'd never learn about vias, which are the primary mechanism for complex routing. Any board they subsequently encounter with via holes would be inexplicable.

The unsafety is specifically that Page 7 APPEARS complete (it has a diagram, measurements, definitions) while BEING incomplete (it shows only the simplest case and doesn't connect structure to purpose).

**Why pairing, not late:** Page 7 causes no confusion when placed early. Its vocabulary is self-introduced ("Silkscreen: Ink text, usually used to mark out components"). It doesn't reference any prior page's terms. It CAN go in the first half — it just can't go ALONE.

**Alone-damage:** If Page 7 is the only structural page a reader sees, they will design single-layer boards when multi-layer boards are needed, because they don't know multi-layer is possible. This is worse than knowing nothing — it's knowing the wrong scope.

**Page 9 — "Electronic Design Automation (EDA) Software"**

**Why pairing, not anchor:** Page 9 LOOKS like a complete tool-selection guide. Three tools compared on multiple criteria (cost, platform, file format, capability). A person encountering it alone might think: "I can now choose the right EDA tool." But this is UNSAFE because:

A reader who has Page 9 without Pages 7-8 will make an ACTIVE BAD DECISION (choosing a tool that can't handle their board's layer requirements) rather than merely having thin knowledge. Bad decisions from false confidence are worse than ignorance.

**Alone-damage:** If Page 9 is the only page a reader sees, they will choose Eagle (free, multi-platform, good libraries) for EVERY project, including high-speed designs where Altium is necessary. ## MANDATORY PAIR WITH NON-INTERCHANGEABLE ORDER

### Pages 7 and 8 — "Structure of a 1-layer PCB board" → "Structure of a (≥2) multi-layer PCB board"

---

**Why they must appear in pair:**

1. **Page 7 alone creates a false ceiling.** Its title says "1-layer" — implying this is the only type. Without Page 8 immediately following, a reader assumes PCBs are single-copper-layer devices. They would then be unable to understand any real-world board with vias (which is virtually ALL boards in consumer electronics). The Novena laptop PCB shown in Page 4 has multiple layers — without Page 8, that board is unexplainable.

2. **Page 8 alone creates a floating extension.** Its opening line — "2-layer board = 2 copper layers, 4-layer board = 4 copper layers, etc" — is an arithmetic pattern that requires a UNIT. That unit (one copper layer containing traces and ground/power plane) is defined ONLY in Page 7. Without Page 7, the equation "2 = 2" has no physical meaning.

3. **The word "too" in Page 7's text ("Usually 1.6mm thick – applies to 2-4 layers too") grammatically REQUIRES Page 8 to follow.** The word "too" is a forward-pointing pronoun: it says "this fact (1.6mm) ALSO applies to the thing I'll describe next." If Page 8 doesn't follow, the "too" points to nothing. If Page 7 is missing and Page 8 stands alone, the "too" references nothing backward either.

4. **Soldermask scope narrowing:** Page 7 defines soldermask as existing on the board surface. Page 8 specifies "Silkscreen and soldermask on top and bottom only." This specification is a NARROWING — it takes the general concept (soldermask exists) and constrains it (only on outer surfaces of multi-layer boards). The narrowing requires the general case to exist first.

---

**Why order cannot be interchanged (8 → 7 is invalid):**

| If 8 comes first | Specific damage |
|---|---|
| "2-layer board = 2 copper layers" | The reader encounters this without knowing what ONE copper layer contains. Is a "copper layer" a solid sheet? A patterned trace network? A mesh? Page 7 answers: "Contains the traces (wires) between components" and "Also contains a ground/power plane." Without this preceding answer, the copper layer is an undefined component in an arithmetic expression. |
| "Blind (only for >2 layer board)" | The reader encounters a via type restricted to ">2 layers" without having first seen what ≤2 layers looks like. The restriction has no reference frame. It's like saying "this feature is only for buildings taller than 2 stories" to someone who has never seen a 1-story building. |
| "Silkscreen and soldermask on top and bottom only" | The reader encounters this restriction without knowing what silkscreen or soldermask ARE. Page 7 defines them: "Silkscreen: Ink text, usually used to mark out components." "Soldermask: Prevent solder from flowing out of designated areas." Without these definitions, the restriction "on top and bottom only" applies to undefined terms. |
| Total Height (1.834mm) | The reader encounters this measurement without knowing the BASELINE (1.6mm from Page 7). They cannot determine whether 1.834mm is thin or thick, standard or unusual. The comparison that gives the number meaning (1.834mm vs. 1.6mm) requires Page 7's number to exist first. |

**Formal test:** Remove Page 7 and give a reader only Page 8. Ask: "What is a copper layer?" They cannot answer from Page 8 alone — it never defines the term, only counts instances of it. Now give a reader only Page 7. Ask: "What is a copper layer?" They CAN answer: "Contains the traces (wires) between components; also contains a ground/power plane." This asymmetry proves that Page 7 is the DEFINING member and Page 8 is the EXTENDING member. Definition must precede extension; the order is non-negotiable.

---

**Under compressed conditions (the stated constraint of this round):**

If only ONE of the pair can be printed and the other must be spoken:
- PRINT Page 7 (the diagram with four labeled layers is difficult to convey orally — "there's a green layer, then a red layer, then a yellow layer, then a lighter green layer" is meaningless without color/position reference)
- SPEAK Page 8 ("The single-layer board we just saw can be stacked: 2 layers means 2 copper layers with vias connecting them. Vias are drilled holes plated with metal. There are three types: blind goes partway down, buried is hidden inside, through-hole goes all the way through.")

This PRESERVES the pair in function while accommodating the page-count compression. But the oral delivery MUST follow the printed Page 7 — never precede it. The order constraint survives even when the medium changes from print to speech.

# NON-EXCHANGEABLE ORDER

---

**Set 1: Page 3 must precede Page 7**

Page 3 defines the PCB's PURPOSE: "A board that lets you attach components to make a circuit." Page 7 defines the PCB's COMPOSITION: "Silkscreen → Soldermask → Copper → Substrate (FR4)." If exchanged (7 before 3), the **OBJECT** changes. The cross-section diagram on Page 7 becomes a materials-science illustration of an unnamed laminate rather than a structural specification of a defined electronic device. The reader knows WHAT layers exist but not WHY they exist — copper carries traces, but traces connect WHAT? Components, to make a circuit — stated only in Page 3. The four layers become an anatomy lesson without a patient. The object shifts from "an electronic interconnection platform with a specific layered structure" to "a layered material of unknown application."

**Set 2: Page 7 must precede Page 8**

Page 7 defines ONE copper layer (traces + ground/power plane, covered by soldermask, labeled by silkscreen, supported by FR-4 substrate). Page 8 COUNTS copper layers (2 = 2, 4 = 4) and defines transitions BETWEEN them (blind, buried, through-hole vias). If exchanged (8 before 7), the **CONDITION** changes. The operating condition of Page 8 shifts from "reader possesses single-layer vocabulary" to "reader possesses no layer vocabulary." Specifically, "Silkscreen and soldermask on top and bottom only" (Page 8) restricts two terms defined in Page 7. Without Page 7 first, this restriction applies to undefined terms — the reader cannot evaluate whether the restriction matters because they don't know what silkscreen or soldermask DO. The condition for comprehension (defined terms) is absent, making Page 8's restrictions formally meaningless.

**Set 3: Page 9 must precede Page 10**

Page 9 establishes the TOOL ENVIRONMENT (Eagle, Altium, KiCad — with library support, file formats, platform limitations). Page 10 specifies the PHYSICAL ENDPOINTS that the tool must accommodate (0603 pads, QFN-48 footprints, USB connectors). If exchanged (10 before 9), the **ROLE** changes. The reader encountering Page 10 first is cast in the role of COMPONENT SHOPPER — someone browsing a parts catalog to select physical components. The reader encountering Page 9 first is cast in the role of TOOL OPERATOR — someone selecting a design environment. With the correct order (9 → 10), Page 10's component dimensions arrive as INPUTS to the selected tool: "Now that you've chosen Eagle, here are the package sizes you'll need to create footprints for." With reversed order, the components arrive as FREE-STANDING physical facts detached from any design workflow. The role shifts from "designer using a tool to place components" to "shopper examining parts without knowing where they'll be used."

**Set 4: Page 1 must precede Page 6**

Page 1 shows the ACTUAL deliverable (555 Blinky board in four stages). Page 6 lists PROMISED deliverables (five bullets including objectives NOT covered in the material). If exchanged (6 before 1), the **COMPLETION STATUS** changes. With the correct order, Page 6's five bullets are bounded by Page 1's visible project — "Design a PCB" means "Design the 555 Blinky." ## GENERAL RULE FOR CHECKING ANY TWO PAGES

When evaluating whether any two pages from this material can be merged into the same main-line position, apply four simultaneous tests:

**Test 1 — Same Object:** Do both pages define, describe, or operate on the same specific object at the same level of abstraction? (Example: Pages 7 and 8 both describe PCB structure, but at different abstraction levels — 1-layer vs. multi-layer. Different levels = different objects for merging purposes.)

**Test 2 — Same Action Target:** Do both pages aim to produce the same change in the reader's state? (Example: Pages 3 and 4 both concern PCBs, but Page 3 aims to DEFINE while Page 4 aims to VALIDATE. Different intended state-changes = different action targets.)

**Test 3 — Same Applicable Conditions:** Do both pages require the same prerequisites and operate under the same assumptions about what the reader already knows? (Example: Pages 5 and 9 both discuss constraints, but Page 5 requires only Page 3 while Page 9 requires Pages 3+7. Different prerequisite sets = different applicable conditions.)

**Test 4 — Same Point in Time:** Do both pages function at the same stage of the workflow — both upstream, both midstream, or both downstream? (Example: Pages 5 and 9 both constrain design, but Page 5 is upstream [deciding whether to make a PCB] while Page 9 is midstream [choosing which tool to design it with]. Different workflow stages = different time points.)

**If and only if all four tests pass simultaneously**, two pages may be merged into the same main-line position. **If any single test fails**, the difference must be documented with reference to visible content in the material itself — not to external common sense — and the pages must remain in separate positions. This rule was constructed from, and is consistent with, the three column-separation criteria established in Round 1 (same question type, same role group, same prerequisites), the five on-site change rulings from Round 2 (especially Change E's prohibition on noun-matching as a merging decision), and the four stability categories from Round 3 (which demonstrated that pages sharing names and visual formats can occupy different categories — Anchor, Reinforcement, Late, Pairing — based on their functional properties rather than their surface features).

## CHANGE E: Conclude that two pages discuss the same object based on shared nouns, similar structure diagrams, the same equipment name, or the same organization name.

**Most likely targets in this material:**

- Pages 7 and 8 share the nouns "silkscreen," "soldermask," "copper," the similar structure diagrams (cross-section layer diagrams), and the same measurement units (mm).
- Pages 1 and 9 share the equipment name "Eagle."
- Pages 3 and 7 share the nouns "copper," "tracks," "substrate," "components."

The proposal: because these pages share surface-level identifiers, they must be "talking about the same object" and can therefore be combined or treated interchangeably.

---

### Box 1: Why it makes people want to do this

Language naturally encourages identity inference. If Page 3 says "copper sheets laminated onto a non-conductive substrate" and Page 7 says "Copper: Contains the traces (wires) between components," a reader sees the word "copper" twice and concludes: "Same object, same page-function." Similarly, Pages 1 and 9 both mention "Eagle" — so surely they're both about Eagle and could be merged or one could replace the other.

This is especially tempting with Pages 7 and 8, which both have layer cross-section diagrams and both mention silkscreen, soldermask, and copper. Someone scanning quickly would say: "These are the same diagram repeated — merge them."

### Box 2: Narrow conditions under which it can be established

Two pages can be concluded to discuss "the same object" **only if** all of the following hold:

1. The shared noun refers to the *same instantiation* of the object — not just the same category. (E.g., "copper" in Page 3 is a definitional category; "copper" in Page 7 is a specific layer in a 1-layer stackup; "copper" in Page 8 is multiple specific layers in a multi-layer stackup. These are three different instantiations.)
2. The pages answer the *same on-site question* about that noun. (Page 3 answers "what is copper's role in a PCB definition?" Page 7 answers "what does the copper layer physically contain?" Page 8 answers "how do multiple copper layers interconnect?" — three different questions.)
3. The pages serve the *same role group* at the *same time point*. (Page 3 serves a novice who doesn't know what a PCB is. Page 7 serves a student who knows the definition but needs specifications. Page 8 serves a student who has single-layer knowledge and needs multi-layer extension.)

**For Pages 7 and 8 specifically:** Condition 1 *appears* met (both discuss copper layers) but is actually violated — Page 7's copper is a *single* layer with traces and a ground/power plane; Page 8's copper is *multiple* layers with via interconnections. These are structurally different objects that happen to share the material name "copper."

**For Pages 1 and 9:** "Eagle" on Page 1 is the *chosen tool for this specific project*. "Eagle" on Page 9 is *one of three compared EDA tools*. Page 1's Eagle is a given; Page 9's Eagle is a choice being evaluated against Altium and KiCad. Different instantiation (project tool vs. market option).

**For Pages 3 and 7:** "Copper" and "substrate" on Page 3 are *definitional categories* within an encyclopedic description. On Page 7 they are *physical layers with measured properties* (FR-4, 1.6mm, fibreglass + epoxy resin). Category vs. instance.

### Box 3: What is missing, what column it damages

**Missing:** Attention to the *functional difference* between pages that share nouns. The shared noun is a **lexical coincidence of reference** — it does not indicate functional identity. What's missing is the distinction between:

- A **definitional reference** to an object (Page 3: "copper sheets" = what category of material)
- A **measurement reference** to an object (Page 7: "Copper: Contains the traces" = what this layer does, physically)
- An **extension reference** to an object (Page 8: multiple copper layers with vias = how instances of this layer relate to each other)

**Column damaged:**

- **If Pages 7 and 8 are combined** (because "same diagrams, same nouns"): The Test Well loses its internal progression from baseline (1-layer) to extension (multi-layer). The Deliverable 4 finding — that Pages 7 and 8 are inseparable but *distinct* — is violated. The 1.6mm carryover statement on Page 8 ("applies to 2-4 layers too") becomes self-referential rather than referencing a prior page's measurement.
- **If Pages 1 and 9 are combined** (because "both mention Eagle"): Principle Road loses its gatekeeper (Page 1 is absorbed into Rework Board). The project identity (555 Blinky, author, dates) gets mixed with tool comparison (Altium cost, KiCad limitations), creating a page that answers two incompatible questions simultaneously.
- **If Pages 3 and 7 are combined** (because "both mention copper and substrate"): The Principle Road secondary gatekeeper (Page 3) is absorbed into Test Well. The foundational definition becomes inseparable from its specification, which means no one can learn "what a PCB is" without simultaneously learning "1.6mm FR-4 fibreglass + epoxy resin." The pedagogical progression from general to specific is destroyed.

**What is destroyed:** The **role division** between pages that *define* an object, pages that *measure* it, pages that *extend* it, and pages that *contextualize* it. Shared nouns ≠ shared function.

### Box 4: Minimal revision to reduce risk

Do not conclude object-identity from shared nouns alone. Instead, apply the three-criteria test from Round 1:

1. Do the pages answer the **same type of on-site question**?
2. Do they serve the **same role group at the same time point**?
3. Do they lack **roughly the same prerequisites**?

If all three are met, the pages may be discussing the same object in the same way. If any one is violated, the shared noun is a **lexical bridge** (connecting pages in sequence) rather than a **functional identity** (making pages interchangeable).

For this material specifically:
- Pages 7 and 8: same question type (✓), same role group (✓), different prerequisites (Page 8 requires Page 7; Page 7 does not require Page 8) → **NOT the same object-function**. They are sequential, not identical.
- Pages 1 and 9: different question type (project identity vs. tool comparison) → **NOT the same object-function** despite shared noun "Eagle."
- Pages 3 and 7: different question type (definition vs. measurement), different role group (novice vs. informed student) → **NOT the same object-function** despite shared nouns "copper" and "substrate."

**Ruling: CAN ONLY BE PARTIALLY RETAINED.**

The partial retention: it is **valid** to note that shared nouns indicate a *sequential dependency* between pages. "Copper" appearing on Pages 3, 7, and 8 correctly identifies that these pages are part of the same conceptual chain. This observation is useful for confirming the main line (Page 1 → 3 → 7 → 8). What **cannot** be retained is the conclusion that shared nouns mean shared function, interchangeability, or combinability. The noun identifies the *thread*; the three-criteria test identifies whether pages on that thread are *functionally distinct nodes* or *redundant duplicates*. In this material, they are always distinct nodes.

# THREE ADDITIONAL PARAGRAPHS

## PARAGRAPH 1: NON-EXCHANGEABLE ORDER

**Set 1: Page 3 must precede Page 7.**

If exchanged (Page 7 before Page 3): the **object** changes. Page 7's "Copper: Contains the traces (wires) between components" uses "traces" as a defined synonym for Page 3's "conductive tracks." If Page 7 arrives first, "traces" is an undefined term — the reader does not know that "trace" = "conductive track" = "wire on a PCB." The object "trace" has no genus. Page 3's role is to provide that genus: "electrically connects electronic components using conductive tracks, pads and other features." Without the genus arriving first, Page 7's species-level measurements describe properties of an unidentified object.

**Set 2: Page 7 must precede Page 8.**

If exchanged (Page 8 before Page 7): the **condition** changes. Page 8's first bullet ("Usually 1.6mm thick – applies to 2-4 layers too") is grammatically conditional on Page 7 having stated the 1.6mm figure for 1-layer boards. The word "too" creates a conditional dependency: "this measurement applies here **as well as** in the previously stated case." If Page 8 arrives first, the condition "previously stated case" has no referent. The "too" points to nothing. Additionally, "Silkscreen and soldermask on top and bottom only" restricts terms that are only defined on Page 7. Without Page 7 first, the restriction "on top and bottom only" restricts undefined terms — a condition applied to nonexistent objects.

**Set 3: Page 9 must precede Page 10.**

If exchanged (Page 10 before Page 9): the **role** changes. Page 10 presents components as an inventory to be *selected from* — the reader's role is "designer choosing packages." But the *ability* to choose depends on tool library availability, which is stated on Page 9: Eagle has "extensive library support," KiCad has "libraries not as common." If Page 10 arrives first, the reader's role is "passive observer of a parts catalog" rather than "active designer constrained by tool availability." The transition from observer to constrained designer is the role change that Page 9 enables — it cannot happen retroactively.

**Set 4: Page 6 must precede Page 7.**

If exchanged (Page 7 before Page 6): the **completion status** changes. Page 6 declares "Understand PCB concepts" as an objective — creating an incomplete status that Page 7 then resolves. If Page 7 arrives first, the reader absorbs specifications without knowing they constitute a *learning objective to be completed*. The completion status "objective pending → objective fulfilled" is replaced by "information received → (no status change)." The material loses its pedagogical progression and becomes an unstructured reference.

**Set 5: Page 4 must precede Page 5.**

If exchanged (Page 5 before Page 4): the **time point** changes. Page 5 lists "Reduce mistakes in manual wiring/soldering" — a motivation that references the *past* practice of manual wiring shown on Page 4. If Page 5 arrives first, "manual wiring/soldering" is referenced as a past practice without the audience having seen that past practice. The time point "this is what used to happen" (Page 4) must precede "this is why we stopped" (Page 5). Reversing them makes Page 5's temporal reference ("reduce mistakes in [something that happened before]") point forward in the sequence rather than backward, breaking chronological coherence.

## PARAGRAPH 2: THE NAMES ARE SIMILAR BUT THE RESPONSIBILITIES ARE DIFFERENT

**Set 1: Page 3 ("copper sheets laminated onto a non-conductive substrate") and Page 7 ("Copper: Contains the traces (wires) between components")**

Both pages use the word "copper" and both reference "substrate." They appear in the same material and discuss the same physical substance. However, they **cannot be placed in the same column** because their responsibilities are categorically different:

- Page 3's responsibility: **define the genus**. "Copper sheets" appears within a definitional sentence that establishes what category of object a PCB belongs to. The responsibility is taxonomic — placing PCBs within the broader world of objects.
- Page 7's responsibility: **measure the species**. "Copper: Contains the traces (wires) between components" appears within a specification list that details what the copper layer physically does, what it contains, and how it relates to other layers. The responsibility is metrological — providing testable, falsifiable properties.

If placed in the same column (Principle Road or Test Well), the distinction between "defining what something is" and "measuring what it does" collapses. The column would simultaneously need to answer "what category?" and "what measurement?" — two different on-site questions serving two different role groups (novice being introduced vs. student seeking specifications). Page 3 belongs to Principle Road. Page 7 belongs to Test Well. The shared noun "copper" is a lexical bridge between columns, not evidence of column identity.

**Set 2: Page 1 ("Introduction to PCB Design (with Eagle)") and Page 9 ("Eagle: Commonly used by makers + Adafruit + Sparkfun")**

Its strengths ("extensive library support") and weaknesses ("not the best for high-speed designs," "User-interface so-so") are listed alongside competitors. The responsibility is enabling an informed choice. Eagle is being evaluated, not declared.

If placed in the same column, the distinction between "this is our tool" (declaration) and "should this be our tool?" (evaluation) collapses. Page 1 belongs to Principle Road (project identity). Page 9 belongs to Rework Board (tool selection/implementation). The shared name "Eagle" connects them sequentially (Page 1 declares, Page 9 evaluates what was declared) but does not make them functionally identical.

## CHANGE E
### "Conclude that two pages are about the same object based on a shared noun, similar structural diagram, the same equipment name, or the same organisation name."

The most available candidates within the ten-page set are:

- **Pages 7 and 8** — both show layer-stack diagrams, both use the words "silkscreen," "soldermask," "copper," and both carry dimensional information about PCB physical structure.
- **Pages 9 and 10** — both are in Wiring Lane, both describe things used inside EDA tools (software on Page 9, component footprints on Page 10), both could be described as "what goes into Eagle."
- **Page 1 and Pages 7–8** — all three show or describe PCB physical structure, and Page 1's board photographs show the same silkscreen/soldermask/copper stack described on Pages 7–8.

**Verdict: CAN ONLY BE PARTIALLY RETAINED** in one specific sub-case; **MUST BE RETURNED** in the others.

---

**Box 1 — Why this change feels compelling**

Shared vocabulary is the most common source of false equivalence in any document set. Pages 7 and 8 both use "copper," "silkscreen," and "soldermask" without adding new definitions for these terms on Page 8 — they are simply re-used. This makes Page 8 appear to be a continuation of Page 7 at the same level of abstraction, rather than an extension that introduces new constraints (via types, multi-layer silkscreen restriction, 1.834mm total height). Similarly, Pages 9 and 10 both live in Wiring Lane, are both "Eagle-adjacent," and both carry library-related content (Page 9 mentions "extensive library support"; Page 10 lists package types that would be found in that library). The shared nouns give the impression that the pages are redundant copies or parallel treatments rather than sequential nodes in a conditional chain.

---

**Box 2 — Narrow conditions under which partial retention could stand**

The *only* sub-case where a shared-noun equivalence argument is partially valid: **Pages 7 and 8 share the same object class** (PCB physical structure) but at different scales of complexity. This means they *could* be treated as a single entry in a reference index (not in a procedural bench) under the label "PCB Layer Structure." That index entry would be valid for look-up purposes. However, as procedural bench nodes, they remain separable because Page 8's content (via types, multi-layer rules) is conditionally unavailable without Page 7's content (the single copper layer definition). They share a noun; they do not share a conditional position.

All other equivalence claims (Pages 9 and 10, Pages 1 and 7–8) must be returned without partial retention.

---

**Box 3 — Missing conditions and column damage**

The critical missing condition in each case:

**Pages 7 and 8:** The shared nouns obscure a *restriction rule* that Page 8 introduces and Page 7 does not contain. Page 7 says silkscreen and soldermask are present on the board (unrestricted). Page 8 says silkscreen and soldermask are on "top and bottom only" (restricted to surface layers in multi-layer boards). This is not the same statement said twice — it is a generalisation and its correction. Treating them as equivalent objects erases the correction.

**Pages 9 and 10:** The shared context (both are used inside Eagle) obscures the fact that Page 9 is a *selection decision* (which tool to use and why, based on constraints) while Page 10 is a *placement resource* (which component footprints exist to be placed once the tool is selected). Selecting a tool and populating it with components are two different procedural events. Page 9 must precede Page 10 because the library availability noted on Page 9 ("extensive library support" for Eagle) is the prerequisite for the component packages on Page 10 being accessible. If they are treated as equivalent, the selection event and the resource event collapse into one simultaneous action, which cannot be executed.

Column damage:

| Column | Damage |
|---|---|
| **Manufacturing Regulations** | Pages 7 and 8 merged → the restriction rule (silkscreen on top/bottom only in multi-layer boards) disappears. The via classification (blind/buried/through-hole) loses its positional grounding in the layer stack. |
| **Wiring Lane** | Pages 9 and 10 merged → tool selection and component placement become simultaneous, eliminating the prerequisite relationship. A designer would attempt to place QFN-48 packages before confirming Eagle Lite's library contains QFN-48 footprints. |

**This destroys the role division between nodes that set conditions and nodes that consume conditions.** Shared nouns are not evidence of shared roles. A rule-setting page and a rule-consuming page may use identical vocabulary — that is how inheritance of vocabulary works across a conditional chain. Identical vocabulary confirms connection, not equivalence.

---

**Box 4 — Minimal revision**

For each suspected equivalence, apply a **three-question filter before merging:**
1. Does one page introduce a term that the other page uses without re-defining? (If yes: they are in a prerequisite relationship, not an equivalence.)
2. Does one page restrict, qualify, or modify a rule stated in the other? (If yes: they are a generalisation-correction pair, not duplicates.)
3. Does one page make a decision that the other page executes? (If yes: they are selection and execution nodes, not parallel entries.)

If any of the three answers is yes, the pages are not equivalent and must remain in separate nodes. Only if all three answers are no — meaning the pages contain truly redundant information about the same object at the same conditional position — can a merge be considered.

## DANGER RANKING: 1 (MOST DANGEROUS) TO 5 (LEAST DANGEROUS)

| Rank | Change | Category of destruction |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **A** — Extract Principle Road's eye-catching page as standalone representative | Destroys the hierarchy |
| **2** | **C** — Move Test Well to the beginning | Destroys the normal/exception page relationship |
| **3** | **B** — Merge Wiring Lane and Manufacturing Regulations | Destroys the conditional boundary |
| **4** | **D** — Use rear page to retroactively determine prior actions | Destroys role division |
| **5** | **E** — Treat shared nouns as evidence of equivalent objects | Local wording/conditional connection problem |

---

### Why Change A earns first place and is sufficient to divert the main line entirely

Change A does not modify one column or one relationship — it removes the **entire conditional chain** by replacing it with a single output image. Page 1 shows the result (finished boards) before showing the process that produced the result. When it is extracted and used as the general representative, the audience receives: a tool name (Eagle), four images of finished artefacts, and an author credit. From this material, they cannot reconstruct what a PCB is (no Page 3), cannot understand what the layers inside it are (no Pages 7–8), cannot select a tool with informed constraints (no Page 9), and cannot identify the components mounted on the visible boards (no Page 10). The main line requires a specific sequence — definition → physical constraint → tool selection → component placement — and Page 1 contains none of those nodes. It is the output of the pipeline, not the pipeline itself. A person handed only Page 1 and asked to design a PCB would have to import the entire missing conditional chain from outside the document, which is exactly what the bench rules prohibit. Every other change in this list disrupts one column or one relationship. Change A disrupts all five columns simultaneously by presenting the endpoint as if it were the entire map.

### Why Change E earns fifth place and is a local wording problem

Change E operates at the level of **vocabulary tagging**, not procedural structure. The shared nouns (copper, silkscreen, Eagle library) are correctly used on both pages where they appear — the problem arises only when a reader draws an equivalence inference from the sharing. That inference is an interpretation error, not a structural error. The bench itself is not changed; the columns are not moved; the gatekeeper pages are not displaced. The only thing that shifts is the reader's internal categorisation of what two pages are *about*. This can be corrected by applying the three-question filter from Box 4 without touching a single column assignment, gatekeeper role, or prerequisite relationship. The damage is local: at worst, two pages within the same column are temporarily misread as redundant, which affects one node in one column. The main line from Page 1 through Page 3 through Pages 7–8 through Pages 9–10 continues to exist and to be executable even while the E-type misreading is present. A local wording correction restores the full function of the bench without restructuring anything.

## PART THREE: PAGES THAT MUST APPEAR IN PAIRS WITH FIXED ORDER

---

### Mandatory Pair Set: Pages 3 → 4 → 5, with internal order fixed

These three pages form a chain rather than a simple pair, but the chain has two specific order locks that cannot be broken independently.

**Lock 1: Page 3 must precede Page 4.**

Page 4's right-hand image is captioned "Modern PCB of Novena laptop." This label deploys "PCB" as a defined term to classify a photographic object. The classification only holds if the audience shares the definition from Page 3. Without that definition, the label either imports outside common sense (which the bench prohibits) or fails to classify the object (making the comparison between wire-wrap and "Modern PCB" a comparison between two unlabelled images). Reversing the order — placing Page 4 before Page 3 — would mean a definition arrives to retroactively ratify a classification that was already made without it. A retroactive definition does not function as a gatekeeper; it functions as an apology. The Test Well's calibration standard must precede the sample it calibrates.

**Lock 2: Page 4 must precede Page 5.**

Page 5 makes four motivational claims. Two of them — "aesthetics" and "durability" — are directly supported by Page 4's visual comparison (the Novena PCB looks clean and professionally finished; the wire-wrap board looks fragile and chaotic). One claim — "making multiple copies / reducing mistakes in manual wiring/soldering" — is directly supported by the wire-wrap image on Page 4, which shows the type of manual wiring that PCBs replace. If Page 5 precedes Page 4, the claims are asserted before their evidence is shown. In a standard motivational sequence, evidence precedes the claim it supports. Here, the four motivations on Page 5 are not self-evident to a person who has never seen wire-wrap construction — they are conclusions from the evidence on Page 4. Reversing the order produces claims that the audience is asked to accept before they have seen the data that justifies them.

**The combined chain Page 3 → 4 → 5 cannot be partially reordered.** Page 3 must be first because it calibrates the Test Well before Page 4 enters it. Page 4 must be second because it provides the evidence before Page 5 claims conclusions from it. The chain has no reversible links.

---

### Mandatory Pair: Pages 7 → 8, with internal order fixed

*(Established as "adjacent pages that cannot be separated" in Round 1, now confirmed as a pairing-with-fixed-order under incompleteness conditions.)*

**Why the pair cannot be split even under compression:** In a compressed session where pages are removed, Pages 7 and 8 must be treated as a single unit. If only one can be taken, Page 7 must be chosen (it is the base-unit anchor; Page 8 is an extension). Page 8 cannot be taken without Page 7, because Page 8 uses "copper layers" in plural, introduces a restriction on "silkscreen and soldermask" that modifies a general rule, and classifies via types by their relationship to a layer stack — all of which require Page 7's vocabulary as their base.

**Why the order cannot be reversed:** Page 8 opens with "2-layer board = 2 copper layers, 4-layer board = 4 copper layers." This counting rule requires that "1 copper layer" already exists as the base unit. That base unit is only established on Page 7. Page 8's silkscreen restriction ("on top and bottom only") is a modification of Page 7's unrestricted statement that silkscreen is a surface layer of the board. A modification cannot precede the rule it modifies.

---

### Mandatory Pair: Pages 8 → 9, with internal order fixed

**Why this pair exists under incompleteness:** Under compressed conditions, someone might consider presenting Page 9 (tool selection) without Page 8 (multi-layer structure), reasoning that the minimum reading package already covers the main line (Pages 1, 3, 7, 9) and Page 8 is reinforcement. But the specific constraint on Page 9 that ties EDA software to physical design — "Eagle Lite supports max 2 copper layers" — requires more than Page 7 alone. It requires Page 8's explicit statement that "2-layer boards good enough for most use-cases" and its introduction of blind and buried via types (which Eagle Lite cannot support). Without Page 8, Page 9's constraint statement claims Eagle Lite is limited to 2 layers, but the audience has no way to evaluate whether this is a serious limitation (it is not, for most use-cases) or a disqualifying one (it is, for high-speed multi-layer designs requiring blind/buried vias). The evaluative context that makes Page 9's constraint actionable lives on Page 8.

**Why the order cannot be reversed:** Page 9 contains "max 2 copper layers" as a constraint on a tool. Page 8 contains the physical and practical context that makes that constraint interpretable ("2-layer boards good enough for most use-cases," blind and buried vias require >2 layers). A constraint stated before the context that governs its severity produces a number that readers either over-interpret (treating 2 layers as an absolute ceiling) or under-interpret (treating it as irrelevant). The constraint must arrive after the context that calibrates it, not before.

## THREE STANDING PARAGRAPHS

---

### NON-EXCHANGEABLE ORDER

The following sets of relationships are fixed. The item listed first must always precede the item listed second. Each set states what changes if the order is reversed.

**Set 1: Page 3 must precede Page 4.**
Page 3 provides the definition of "PCB." Page 4's right-hand image is captioned "Modern PCB of Novena laptop." If Page 4 precedes Page 3, the label deploys the term "PCB" before its definition exists in the document. What changes is the **condition**: the Test Well's calibration standard disappears. The measurement (is the right-hand image a PCB?) cannot be performed without the standard (what is a PCB?). Once Page 4 precedes Page 3, the comparison becomes an appeal to outside common sense, which the bench prohibits. Reversing the order does not merely resequence information — it removes the condition under which the label on Page 4 carries technical meaning.

**Set 2: Page 7 must precede Page 8.**
Page 7 introduces the singular copper layer as a base unit. Page 8 counts copper layers ("2-layer board = 2 copper layers") and classifies via types by their relationship to those layers. If Page 8 precedes Page 7, the base unit of the counting operation has never been defined. What changes is the **object**: "copper layers" on Page 8 is a plural of an object that has not been introduced as a singular. The via definition — "hole that electrically connects points between copper layers" — describes a relationship between objects whose individual properties are unknown. Additionally, Page 8's restriction ("silkscreen and soldermask on top and bottom only") modifies a general rule from Page 7; reversing the order means the restriction appears before the rule it restricts, making the restriction uninterpretable.

**Set 3: Pages 7–8 must precede Page 9.**
Pages 7–8 establish the physical layer vocabulary and the practical layer-count guideline. Page 9 constrains tool selection by reference to that vocabulary ("Eagle Lite: max 2 copper layers"). If Page 9 precedes Pages 7–8, the constraint number "2 copper layers" has no physical referent and no evaluative context. What changes is **resources**: the resource decision on Page 9 (Eagle Lite: free but constrained; Altium: US$10K/license but unconstrained; KiCad: free and unconstrained) can only be made with knowledge of what design complexity is required. That complexity is determined by Pages 7–8 (specifically: "2-layer boards good enough for most use-cases" from Page 8, and the blind/buried via requirements from Page 8). Without Pages 7–8 first, the resource allocation on Page 9 is made without knowing what it is purchasing.

**Set 4: Page 5 must precede Page 6.**
Page 5 provides the motivational cause for the manufacturing and assembly pipeline. Page 6 declares five session objectives, the fourth of which is "Send for manufacturing" and the fifth of which is "Efficient SMD assembling techniques." If Page 6 precedes Page 5, these two objectives appear before the motivational argument that generates them. What changes is the **time point**: the scope declaration on Page 6 is a forward-projection event that belongs at the transition between the motivational block and the technical block. Moving it before Page 5 means the scope is declared before the motivation is established, converting the objectives from "goals that follow from our reasons" into "goals that precede our reasons" — which makes the session appear to be asserting conclusions before its own arguments have been made.

**Set 5: Page 4 must precede Page 5.**
Page 4 provides cited empirical evidence (two external sources). Page 5 makes four motivational claims, two of which ("durability," "aesthetics") are directly grounded in Page 4's visual comparison. If Page 5 precedes Page 4, the claims arrive before the evidence that supports them. What changes is the **completion status**: on Page 5, the claim "PCBs offer durability advantages over wire-wrapping" should have the status of a conclusion drawn from Page 4's evidence. If Page 5 is read first, that claim has the status of an unverified assertion. When Page 4 then arrives, it no longer functions as evidence for the claims — the claims have already been received as asserted rather than as evidence-dependent conclusions. The completion status of the motivational argument is permanently misread.

### THE NAMES ARE SIMILAR BUT THE RESPONSIBILITIES ARE DIFFERENT

The following sets of pages share vocabulary, visual similarity, or subject-adjacent content but cannot be placed in the same column because their procedural roles, question types, and prerequisite chains are different.

**Set 1: Page 7 (Manufacturing Regulations) and Page 9 (Wiring Lane)**

Both pages make specific statements about the number of copper layers in a PCB design. Page 7 states "usually 1.6mm thick — applies to 2-4 layers too" and introduces the copper layer as a named physical object. Page 9 states "Eagle Lite: supports max 2 copper layers." The shared noun is "copper layers" and the shared numeric range (1–4) appears to make these pages equivalent treatments of the same constraint.

They are not equivalent. Page 7 states a material property of the manufactured artefact — the copper layer is a physical stratum of the board that exists regardless of which tool designed it. This is a Manufacturing Regulations statement: it describes what the object is made of. Page 9 states a software limitation of a specific tool — Eagle Lite can only produce routing files for designs with up to 2 copper layers. This is a Wiring Lane statement: it describes what the instrument can handle. A designer who switches from Eagle Lite to Altium Designer does not change the physical nature of the copper layer described on Page 7. The physical constraint (copper exists as a layer in the board) is permanent; the tool constraint (Eagle Lite handles max 2 of those layers) is contingent on tool selection. Placing both pages in Manufacturing Regulations would convert a tool limitation into a physical law. Placing both in Wiring Lane would convert a material property into a software specification. Neither is correct.

**Set 2: Page 5 (Principle Road) and Page 4 (Test Well)**

Both pages address the question of why a PCB is preferable to alternatives, and both appear in consecutive positions in the reading sequence. Page 5 lists four motivations including "Durability" and "Aesthetics." Page 4 shows a visual comparison between wire-wrap construction and a modern PCB, with durability and aesthetics visually implied by the contrast between the chaotic wire-wrap and the clean finished board.

They cannot occupy the same column. Page 4 is a Test Well calibration node: it presents cited photographic evidence from two external sources, positions the audience as observers evaluating a comparison between two physical artefacts, and answers a historical-comparative question (what did construction look like before PCBs, and what does it look like now?). Page 5 is a Principle Road motivation node: it presents an asserted list without citations, positions the audience as practitioners deciding whether to adopt PCB design, and answers a personal-decision question (why should a maker pursue this approach?). The Round 1 contamination rule states that a Test Well page must show a counterpart or evidence; a Principle Road page makes claims. Page 4 shows; Page 5 claims. They are not two angles on the same topic — they are two different procedural operations that happen to share subject matter. The subject matter similarity is exactly the reason the distinction must be stated explicitly in the handover.

### CAN BE DISPLAYED SIDE BY SIDE, BUT FOOTNOTES CANNOT BE LOST

The following sets of pages may appear together in a compressed or parallel presentation, but restrictions, boundaries, and subsequent explanations must be retained even when the pages are displayed simultaneously.

**Set 1: Pages 7 and 8 (both Manufacturing Regulations)**

These two pages can be displayed side by side as a single "PCB Layer Structure" unit in a compressed session. Their content is directly continuous: Page 7 introduces the single-layer stack; Page 8 extends it to multi-layer configurations. A side-by-side display allows an audience to see the progression from 1-layer to ≥2-layer without a slide transition.

The restriction that cannot be lost: the internal reading order is fixed at Page 7 first, Page 8 second, even in a side-by-side display. The base-unit vocabulary (single copper layer, silkscreen as a surface feature without restriction) must be received before the extension vocabulary (plural copper layers, silkscreen restricted to top and bottom). If the two pages are displayed side by side without a declared reading order, an audience member who begins reading Page 8 will encounter the restriction ("silkscreen and soldermask on top and bottom only") before receiving the general rule it restricts (silkscreen is a surface layer of the board). The subsequent explanation that must be retained is: Page 8's silkscreen restriction is a modification of Page 7's general statement, not a standalone rule. Additionally, the via classification on Page 8 (blind, buried, through-hole) must be footnoted as requiring Page 7's copper-layer base unit for the definitions to be grounded.

**Set 2: Pages 9 and 10 (both Wiring Lane)**

These two pages can be displayed side by side as a single "Design Tools and Components" unit in a compressed session. Page 9's tool selection (Eagle, with library noted as "extensive") and Page 10's component package list (0603, 0805, QFN-48, etc.) are directly adjacent in the design workflow: choose a tool, then identify which components its library contains.

The restriction that cannot be lost: the prerequisite chain for this pairing (Pages 7, 8 must already be in place) cannot be omitted simply because the two Wiring Lane pages are displayed together. When side by side, Page 9's "max 2 copper layers" constraint looks self-contained — a reader seeing it alongside Page 10's package list might conclude that the constraint is a library limitation rather than a physical-layer limitation. The footnote that must be retained: "max 2 copper layers" on Page 9 is a tool constraint on a physical object whose nature was defined on Page 7 and whose practical sufficiency was confirmed on Page 8. Without that footnote, the constraint appears as an arbitrary Eagle specification rather than as a response to a physical design requirement. Additionally, Page 10's component packages (specifically multi-pad ICs like QFN-48 and SSOP-28) have via and layer implications that only become apparent when Pages 7–8 are cited as the grounding context. The subsequent explanation that must be retained: component placement on Page 10 occurs within the layer constraints described on Pages 7–8, and within the library constraints described on Page 9; none of these three constraints can be read as independent of the other two.

**Step 1 — Establish the visual anchor before any definition.**

**ONE GENERAL RULE**

*This rule applies to any two pages in the current set or any future pages added to the bench. It is the single test for whether a merge is admissible.*

> **If two pages share the same object, the same action target, the same applicable conditions, and the same point in time, they may be considered for merging into the same main line node. If any one of these four elements differs between the two pages, the difference must be explicitly stated and the pages must remain in separate nodes — they cannot be merged directly.**

Application examples from this set:

Pages 7 and 8 share the same **object** (PCB physical structure) but differ in **applicable conditions** (Page 7 applies to all boards; Page 8 applies only when the layer count exceeds one) and **point in time** (Page 7 is the base-unit introduction; Page 8 is the extension that presupposes the base unit). One difference is sufficient to prevent merging. Two differences confirm the separation.

Pages 9 and 10 share the same **action target** (operating within an EDA tool) but differ in **object** (Page 9's object is the tool itself; Page 10's object is the component footprints that populate the tool), **applicable conditions** (Page 9 requires layer vocabulary from Pages 7–8; Page 10 requires all of Pages 7, 8, and 9), and **point in time** (Page 9 is the selection event; Page 10 is the execution event). Three differences are present. The pages are connected but not equivalent and must remain in separate nodes.

Pages 4 and 5 share the same **point in time** (pre-design motivational phase) but differ in **object** (Page 4's object is cited photographic evidence; Page 5's object is an asserted claim list), **action target** (Page 4 targets an observing evaluator; Page 5 targets a deciding practitioner), and **applicable conditions** (Page 4 requires only Page 3; Page 5 requires both Page 3 and Page 4). Three differences. Separate columns, non-negotiable.

### RESULT 3 — SUSPENSION AREA

**Suspended pages: PAGE 2 and PAGE 4**

**PAGE 2 (*About Me*):**
Page 2 cannot enter the main technical line because it answers a question about *roles* (who is this person?) rather than about objects, structures, constraints, or verification states. It does not advance the PCB content. However, it cannot be deleted because it provides the credential foundation for every factual claim in Pages 3 onward. ### RESULT 4A — ADJACENT PAGES THAT CANNOT BE SEPARATED

**Pages 7 and 8** (*1-layer structure* and *≥2-layer structure*)

These two pages must travel together. **Evidence from the material itself:**

Page 7 introduces: substrate, copper layer (singular), soldermask, silkscreen, and the 1.6mm thickness figure.

Page 8 opens with: "2-layer board = 2 copper layers" — this statement only makes mathematical and conceptual sense if the audience just learned what one copper layer is. Page 8 then introduces vias as *holes that connect copper layers* — this definition requires the copper layer concept Page 7 just delivered. Page 8's cross-section diagram shows "Top Layer" and "Bottom Layer" separated by core and prepreg — these labels are shorthand for the full layer description on Page 7.

Separating them — for example by inserting Page 9 (EDA tools) between them — would force the audience to receive tool constraints (max 2 copper layers in Eagle Lite) before they have finished understanding what a copper layer physically is. The structural argument is one continuous movement from simple (single layer) to complex (multi-layer + vias), and the two pages share a single on-site question ("what is inside the PCB physically?"), the same audience state (they are mid-structure-explanation), and the same prerequisite (Page 3's PCB definition). All three criteria for co-location are met, and no criterion changes between them.

---

### RESULT 4B — ADJACENT PAGES THAT CANNOT BE COMBINED

**Pages 6 and 7** (*Objective of lesson* and *Structure of a 1-layer PCB board*)

These appear consecutively and may seem combinable — Page 6 lists what will be learned, Page 7 starts delivering it. They cannot be merged. **Evidence from the material itself:**

Page 6 belongs to Station D (Test Well). It answers: "Is the audience aligned with the session's success criteria before technical content begins?" The on-site question is *verificational and prospective.*

Page 7 belongs to Station B (Wiring Lane). It answers: "What is physically inside a PCB layer-by-layer?" The on-site question is *structural and descriptive.*

The *role* they serve is different: Page 6 serves the audience-as-evaluator (they are checking whether they understand what they are about to measure themselves against), while Page 7 serves the audience-as-learner (they are receiving first-time technical content). The *time point* is different: Page 6 occurs before any technical claim is made; Page 7 is the first technical claim. The *prerequisite state* is different: Page 6 requires only that motivation has been established (Pages 1–5); Page 7 requires that the lesson frame has been set (Page 6).

Combining them would force the verification checkpoint and the first technical delivery to occupy the same moment — which destroys the checkpoint's function. A checkpoint cannot simultaneously be the thing being checked. The pages are adjacent because one immediately enables the other, but they are on different stations and serve different role-moment-prerequisite combinations.

# TINY CIRCUIT CITY PAVEMENT — ROUND 2 ON-SITE CHANGE RULINGS

*Lab bench from Round 1 is held fixed. Column names, gatekeeper assignments, and station definitions are unchanged. All five rulings operate inside those frozen constraints.*
