## PART ONE: THE FOUR MISSION CARDS

---

### 🃏 CARD A — "STONE CRADLE" (Controlled Training Wall Commission)

| Field | Specification |
|---|---|
| **Card Name** | Stone Cradle |
| **Suitable Climbing Site** | Artificial climbing walls (indoor gym walls, inflatable walls, outdoor constructed training walls with pre-set holds) |
| **Required Protection Method** | Top-rope belay mandatory; harness + helmet required; auto-belay or human belayer on ground; rated anchor points pre-installed |
| **Minimum Entry Requirement** | Guild Level: **Hatchling (Lv.0)**. No prior climbing experience needed. Must attend 10-minute ground safety brief. Must wear closed-toe shoes. |
| **Unacceptable External Scenes** | Natural rock of any kind, ice, industrial scaffolding, open-air ridgelines, canyon interiors, any surface above 2 stories without engineered fall zone |
| **Mutually Exclusive Tag** | 🏷️ *Manufactured Surface Only* — the climbing medium must be human-fabricated. If any portion of the route is unmodified natural stone, this card is void. |

---

### 🃏 CARD B — "RED WALL" (Natural Rock Wall Commission)

| Field | Specification |
|---|---|
| **Card Name** | Red Wall |
| **Suitable Climbing Site** | Outdoor natural rock faces — sandstone, limestone, granite sport crags or trad crags with bolt lines or trad gear placements |
| **Required Protection Method** | Lead rope or top-rope with quickdraws/cams/nuts; helmet strongly recommended; belayer must be certified; minimum two-person team |
| **Minimum Entry Requirement** | Guild Level: **Rope Runner (Lv.2)**. Must have completed ≥ 20 indoor top-rope sessions + 5 outdoor top-rope sessions. Must demonstrate clipping, fall arrest, and knot-tying competency. |
| **Unacceptable External Scenes** | Indoor/artificial walls, ice of any form, industrial buildings, rooftops, inflatable structures, canyon slots narrower than 1.5 m |
| **Mutually Exclusive Tag** | 🏷️ *Geological Surface + Recreational/Sport Purpose* — the climb must be on unmodified natural rock AND the purpose must be sport/recreation/training, not industrial or rescue. If the purpose is commercial construction work, this card is void. |

---

### 🃏 CARD C — "Frozen Fang" (Ice Wall Commission)

| Field | Specification |
|---|---|
| **Card Name** | Frozen Fang |
| **Suitable Climbing Site** | Natural or artificial ice falls, frozen waterfalls, glacial seracs, mixed ice-rock faces |
| **Required Protection Method** | Dual ice axes (technical tools); crampons rated for vertical ice; ice screws placed by leader; rope + harness + helmet mandatory; cold-weather layering system |
| **Minimum Entry Requirement** | Guild Level: **Frost Fang (Lv.3 specialty)**. Must hold Red Wall (Lv.2) certification AND complete a guild-approved ice clinic (≥ 3 days). Must demonstrate self-arrest, ice-screw placement, and crampon technique. |
| **Unacceptable External Scenes** | Any rock-only surface, any artificial wall, any urban/industrial setting, any scene without visible ice or frozen medium |
| **Mutually Exclusive Tag** | 🏷️ *Frozen Medium + Specialized Steel Tools* — the climbing surface must be ice/frozen water AND the climber must use ice-specific tools (axes, crampons, screws). If axes are absent or the surface is dry rock, this card is void. |

---

### 🃏 CARD D — "Scaffold Ghost" (Industrial / Structural Height Operations Commission)

| Field | Specification |
|---|---|
| **Card Name** | Scaffold Ghost |
| **Suitable Climbing Site** | Building exteriors, rooftops, scaffolding, bridges, towers, industrial structures requiring height access for maintenance, repair, or inspection |
| **Required Protection Method** | Fall-arrest harness (EN 361 or equivalent); lanyard with shock absorber; hard hat (not climbing helmet); anchor to structural steel or certified tie-off point; scaffolding or aerial lift as primary access where possible |
| **Minimum Entry Requirement** | Guild Level: **Iron Wraith (Lv.3 specialty, industrial track)**. Must hold nationally recognized Working at Heights certification. NOT interchangeable with recreational climbing levels. Employer liability documentation required. |
| **Unacceptable External Scenes** | Any natural rock, ice, artificial climbing wall, canyon, or recreational climbing setting. Any scene where the primary purpose is sport or training. |
| **Mutually Exclusive Tag** | 🏷️ *Man-Made Structure + Occupational Purpose* — the surface must be a building/infrastructure AND the activity must be work (repair, inspection, construction). If the person is climbing for recreation on the same structure, this card is void; it becomes trespassing, not a commission. |

#### Why These Cannot Be Combined by Height Alone:

| Factor | Ice Wall (Img 2) | Canyon Slot (Img 5) | Natural Outer Rock (Img 7) | Roof/Building (Img 4) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Medium** | Frozen water — ephemeral, temperature-dependent | Confined rock — narrow, wet, dark | Open rock face — exposed, weathered | Brick/concrete — structural, load-bearing |
| **Primary Hazard** | Icefall, hypothermia, tool failure, ice quality collapse | Flash flood, entrapment, rockfall in confined space, limited escape | Rockfall, weather exposure, long rescue approach, loose rock | Structural collapse, falling objects, electrical lines, public below |
| **Tool Set** | Ice axes, crampons, ice screws — **unique to ice** | Rappel device, fixed-line ascenders, canyon-specific anchors | Quickdraws/cams/nuts, standard rock rack | Fall-arrest lanyard, scaffold clamps, hard hat — **unique to industry** |
| **Escape Method** | Rappel on V-threads or screw anchors; may require ice bollard | Ascend rope out or continue through; cannot reverse in water | Walk off, rappel established route, or helicopter | Scaffold descent, aerial lift, ladder — infrastructure-dependent |
| **Governing Authority** | Alpine/mountaineering club certification | Canyoneering permit, park authority | Climbing access agreements, crag ethic | OSHA/HSE occupational safety regulation |
| **Why Height Alone Fails** | Height is irrelevant if ice quality is poor at 3m — a 3m ice climb can kill via icefall. Height ≠ danger here. | Canyon danger is about CONFINEMENT, not height. A 5m slot can be lethal in a flash flood regardless of vertical distance. | The distance in Image 7 makes height seem dramatic but obscures actual risk, which depends on rock quality and protection at the individual level. | Height is regulated by scaffolding standards, not climbing grades. A 4m wall with no scaffold is more dangerous than a 20m wall with proper staging. |

**Conclusion: Each environment has a UNIQUE LETHAL MECHANISM that is not altitude-dependent. Combining them under a single "height" metric would erase the specific expertise required to survive each one.**

## PART FIVE: DOWNGRADE RULING

### 📉 Selected Conclusion for Downgrade: **IMAGE 6 — Vista Ridge Scramble**

**Current Status:** Registered under Card B — "Red Wall" (Vista sub-type), assessed as potential Lv.2 environmental evidence.

**Ruling: DOWNGRADED to "Can Only Be Retained For Now"**

**Reason:**

Image 6 shows a young woman on an exposed rocky ridge with a stunning panoramic valley behind her. She holds what appears to be a fixed cable (via ferrata rail or chain). However:

1. **No harness is visible.** A via ferrata requires a Y-lanyard harness system clipped to the cable at all times. Without it, the cable is merely a handhold, not protection.
2. **No helmet is visible.** The exposed ridge has loose rock above and a catastrophic fall consequence below.
3. **Casual clothing (cotton sweater, cotton shorts, ankle socks).** These suggest a day-hiker, not a prepared climber. No climbing shoes, no layering for weather change at altitude.
4. **No rope, no partner, no belay of any kind.** She is unroped, alone (or photographer only), and unprotected on a position where a single slip means a multi-hundred-meter fall.

**What visual evidence is missing before upgrade is possible:**

| Missing Evidence | Why It Matters |
|---|---|
| Visible harness + via ferrata Y-lanyard clipped to cable | Would prove she is protected against falls; without it, this is an unprotected scramble, not a climbing commission |
| Helmet | Would demonstrate awareness of rockfall hazard on an exposed ridge |
| Climbing or approach shoes (rigid sole, ankle support) | Would indicate prepared mountaineering rather than casual hiking beyond her preparation level |
| Second person / belayer or via ferrata partner | Guild rules require minimum two-person team for any outdoor natural rock commission |
| Close-up of the cable/anchor system | Would confirm whether the fixed installation is a rated via ferrata or simply an old agricultural chain

### RULING: 🔴 REJECTED

**The appeal fundamentally confuses the verb "climbing" with the noun "climbing commission."** The fact that a person ascends a vertical surface does not make the activity a climbing commission under the guild's system. A window washer climbs. A firefighter on a ladder climbs. A child climbing a tree climbs. None of these are Card B commissions.

Card B's identity is defined by THREE simultaneous conditions:
1. **Geological surface** (natural rock)
2. **Recreational/sport purpose**
3. **Climbing-specific protection** (rope, harness, anchors, belayer)

Image 4 fails ALL THREE. Reclassifying it to Card B would:
- Violate the Manufactured Surface exclusion
- Violate the Occupational Purpose exclusion
- Create a precedent where any vertical movement on any surface qualifies as rock climbing
- Erase the legal distinction between workplace safety regulation and recreational risk acceptance

**Aggravating Factor:** Image 4 already carries a **Red Flag annotation** from Round 1 for visible safety violations (no PPE in an occupational setting). Moving it to Card B would not erase the violation — it would merely disguise it as a recreational choice rather than a regulatory breach, which is worse.

The appeal is **unsalvageable in its current form.** However, if the applicant's TRUE intent is to create a new commission type for "urban climbing / buildering as recreation," the following would be required:

| Condition | Current State | Required Change |
|---|---|---|
| Surface | Brick building (man-made) | Would need to remain Card D OR a new Card E "Urban Ascent" would need to be chartered — Card B cannot absorb it |
| Purpose | Occupational (hi-vis, scaffold) | The climber would need to be in recreational clothing, with NO hi-vis, NO scaffold, and NO employer relationship |
| Protection | None visible | Full sport climbing harness, rope, bolted anchors on building (with property owner's written permission) |
| Legal framework | Workplace safety | Would need recreational liability waiver + trespass clearance |

**Even with all these changes, the result would NOT be Card B. It would require a new card type entirely, which is beyond the scope of this appeal.**

### RULING: ⬇️ DOWNGRADED (to "Same Shelf Display Only — Thematic Pairing")

The appeal is **not approved as action proof** but is **partially salvageable** as a shelf display.

**Why Not Rejected Outright:**
The applicant's instinct — that a wide establishing shot and a close-up detail shot have documentary value when shown together — is not wrong in principle. Film and photojournalism use this technique constantly. The error is in claiming **evidentiary equivalence** (that one proves the other) rather than **thematic complementarity** (that they tell a richer story together).

**Downgrade Terms:**

Image 7 and Image 9 may be **displayed on the same shelf** under the heading:

> **"Natural Rock Environments — Context and Detail"**

With the following mandatory shelf footnote:

Image 7 provides environmental scale; Image 9 provides technical detail. However, NO location match, person match, or time match has been established. Image 7 CANNOT serve as proof that Image 9's climb occurred at the depicted crag. Image 9 CANNOT serve as proof that the distant figures in Image 7 are climbing competently. Each image retains its independent classification: Image 7 = Scene Survey (unverifiable); Image 9 = Card B Sport Lead (verified close-up).*

### MINIMUM REVISED VERSION (What Would Make This Approvable as Action Proof):

| Missing Evidence | What It Would Provide |
|---|---|
| A **mid-range photo** showing the specific route on the cliff with Image 9's climber identifiable (white t-shirt, body type) on the wall | Bridges the gap between "distant speck" and "close-up hands" |
| **GPS metadata** on both images showing identical coordinates | Proves same location |
| A **route topo or guidebook page** visible in one image or referenced in both | Names the specific route and confirms the crag |
| A **group photo at the base** showing Image 9's climber with the cliff from Image 7 recognizable behind them | Connects person to place at human-verifiable scale |

**Without at least ONE of these bridging elements, the action-proof claim cannot be approved.**

This is the **most dangerous appeal** received by the tribunal. If approved, it would create a precedent where a child's introductory wall session is accepted as a prerequisite for expert-level ice climbing. This is not a procedural objection — it is a **life-safety objection.**

**Specific Grounds for Rejection:**

1. **Person mismatch:** Irrefutably different individuals (child vs. adult). No progression narrative is possible.
2. **Five-level gap:** The guild's progression system requires each intermediate level to be individually earned and documented. Direct Lv.0 → Lv.3 specialty is categorically prohibited.
3. **Zero skill transfer:** Artificial wall climbing develops no ice-specific skills. The tool sets (hands on plastic holds vs. ice axes on frozen water) share nothing.
4. **Mutually exclusive card tags violated:** Card A (Manufactured Surface) and Card C (Frozen Medium) are the most distant pair in the guild's system. They share no surface, no tool, no environment, no skill, and no risk profile.
5. **Environmental lethality gap:** The artificial wall (Image 3) has near-zero environmental lethality (padded floor, staff, top-rope). The ice wall (Image 2) has extreme environmental lethality (icefall, hypothermia, tool failure, ice collapse). Bridging this gap requires years of progressive exposure, not a single card swap.

**This appeal cannot be saved by changing one condition.** It requires a fundamentally different chain:

    ↓ [ADD: Lv.2 outdoor top-rope on rock — Image 1 serves]
    ↓ [ADD: Lv.2 lead on rock — Image 9 serves]

Image 2 (Card C)
```

**Minimum images needed between Image 3 and Image 2:** At least **3 intermediate images** (outdoor rock top-rope, outdoor rock lead, ice clinic with instructor) plus documentation of the ice clinic completion. The current image set provides Image 1 and Image 9 for the middle steps, but the ice clinic is entirely absent.

### STEP 1: Begin with COLUMN 1 — TRAINING WALLS (Images 3 & 8)

**Why Start Here:**
Every guild member's journey begins at the training wall. This column contains the lowest-risk, most controlled images. It establishes the BASELINE: what "climbing" looks like when every variable is managed — artificial surface, pre-set holds, top-rope, staff supervision, padded floors.

**Card Swap Vulnerability Referenced:**
⚠️ **Appeal C (REJECTED)** attempted to jump directly from this column (Image 3, training wall) to Column 3 (Image 2, ice wall). The tribunal ruled this impossible because five levels and one specialty clinic are bypassed. Beginning here reminds the administrator that **this column is the FLOOR, not the CEILING** — and that no one leaves this column without intermediate documentation.

**What to Notice:**
- Image 8 (inflatable) and Image 3 (rigid) sit side by side but are sub-type separated (Soft Structure vs. Rigid Wall)
- Image 3 has an equipment deficiency flag (no helmet) — this is the earliest sign that LOOKING like you're climbing ≠ BEING properly equipped to climb
- Neither image alone is sufficient for Lv.1 advancement

---

### STEP 2: Jump to COLUMN 6 — VISTA CAMPS (Images 6 & 7)

**Why Go Here Second (Not Column 2):**
This is the **TRAP COLUMN** — the column that looks most impressive but proves the least. By showing it EARLY, the administrator learns to distinguish between "dramatic altitude imagery" and "verified climbing competency" before they encounter the formal columns.

**Card Swap Vulnerability Referenced:**
⚠️ **Appeal B (DOWNGRADED)** attempted to use Image 7 (this column) as "action proof" for Image 9 (Column 2). The tribunal ruled that an image tagged "Unverifiable Distance" cannot prove individual action. **The lesson: grandeur is not evidence.**

⚠️ **Image 6's Round 1 Downgrade** established that visible altitude + natural rock + a person ≠ a climbing commission. The missing elements (harness, helmet, shoes, partner) are INVISIBLE from a distance — which is exactly why this column exists separately from formal commissions.

**What to Notice:**
- Both images are visually spectacular but informationally empty
- Image 7 could be mistaken for proof of multi-pitch rock climbing (Appeal B's exact error)
- Image 6 could be mistaken for via ferrata competency (but no harness is visible)
- This column teaches: **the camera's position ≠ the subject's qualification**

---

### STEP 3: Proceed to COLUMN 2 — NATURAL ROCK WALLS (Images 1, 9, 10)

**Why Here Third:**
Having seen the floor (Column 1) and the trap (Column 6), the administrator now encounters the CORE PROGRESSION — the three images that form the guild's primary upgrade chain (top-rope → sport lead → trad lead). This is the column with the most internal hierarchy and the most clearly documented card replacements.

**Card Swap Vulnerability Referenced:**
⚠️ **Round 2 Upgrade Chain 2** (Image 1 → Image 9 → Image 10) establishes the only fully approved vertical replacement sequence in the registry. Each step is a REAL upgrade:
- 1→9: Top-rope to lead (fall-factor management gained)
- 9→10: Sport to trad (self-placed protection gained)

⚠️ **Appeal D (DOWNGRADED)** attempted to connect Column 1's Image 3 to this column's Image 1 as "same novice's journey." The tribunal denied person-matching but approved the CONCEPTUAL sequence. This column's Image 1 IS the valid entry point from Column 1 — but only with proper intermediate documentation.

**What to Notice:**
- Image 1 is GROUP supervised (Custodian role filled by belayer); Image 9 is individual sport lead; Image 10 is individual trad lead with headlamp
- The progression from "someone else manages my safety" → "I clip pre-installed bolts" → "I CREATE my own safety system" is the deepest skill evolution in the guild
- Image 10 is the only image in the entire registry that the tribunal has not flagged for ANY deficiency — it is the gold standard

### STEP 4: Move to COLUMN 4 — CANYON CREVICES (Image 5)

**Why Here Fourth:**
After seeing the open-face rock wall progression, the administrator now encounters a LATERAL specialization — same card (Card B), same medium (natural rock), but completely different geometry, direction of travel, and hazard profile. This column teaches that "natural rock" is not monolithic.

**Card Swap Vulnerability Referenced:**

- Image 10 uses SELF-PLACED gear (building a system)
- "Using" and "building" are fundamentally different skill types

## Volume I: Card Establishment, Image Registration, Upgrade Chains, and Mutual Exclusion Protocol

# PART ONE — FOUR MISSION CARDS

---

## 🟢 CARD 1 — [STONE FROG] · Artificial Wall Initiation

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Suitable Sites** | Indoor climbing gyms · outdoor artificial hold walls · inflatable portable event walls · carnival climbing towers |
| **Required Protection** | Top-rope mandatory at all times; auto-belay device OR certified human belayer; full harness (waist + leg loops both locked); helmet strongly recommended, non-compliance must be noted by supervising staff |
| **Minimum Entry** | Zero prior experience acceptable; must pass harness-fit check by staff before mounting; body weight within wall's rated load; minors must have guardian sign liability waiver; no minimum age if guardian is on-site |
| **Unacceptable External Scenes** | Natural rock surfaces of any kind · ice or frozen surfaces · scaffolding structures · canyon gaps · uneven terrain · any visible free drop greater than 2 m without enclosure · industrial PPE worn by climber |

---

## 🔵 CARD 2 — [IRON FIST] · Natural Rock Wall Commission

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Suitable Sites** | Outdoor sport-climbing crags · trad routes · sequential group-route cliffs · via ferrata fixed-line ridges · boulder fields with crash pads |
| **Required Protection** | Helmet + harness both mandatory (no exceptions); lead rope or top-rope anchored to natural or fixed protection; belayer must be guild-certified or directly supervised by certified member; anchor inspection before each session |
| **Minimum Entry** | Completion of Card 1 or equivalent logbook of ≥ 10 sessions; demonstrated ability to fall safely; ability to identify at least two anchor types; age 12+ unaccompanied, age 6+ with certified adult partner on the same route |
| **Unacceptable External Scenes** | Inflatable or soft surfaces · scaffolding frames · ice tools of any kind · industrial hi-vis vest worn by climber · enclosed canyon geometry where both walls press the body simultaneously · urban skyline as primary backdrop |

---

## 🔴 CARD 3 — [WHITE FANG] · Extreme Environment Strike

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Suitable Sites** | Ice waterfalls · frozen rock faces · canyon crevices · narrow slot canyons · underground chimney routes |
| **Required Protection** | **Ice sub-type:** paired ice axes + crampons + full-body harness + chin-locked helmet + insulated outer layer rated to local temperature. **Canyon sub-type:** static rope + canyon-specific anchor system + full harness + helmet + emergency communication device. **Both sub-types:** Solo operations absolutely forbidden; partner system required at all times |
| **Minimum Entry** | Card 2 completed + successful completion of an environment-specific course; cold-weather self-arrest certification (ice) OR confined-space awareness certification (canyon); emergency contact registered with guild before departure |
| **Unacceptable External Scenes** | Artificial walls of any type · urban building skylines · children operating without certified adult · crowd-observation context · open panoramic horizon without visible canyon walls or ice formation · recreational rope systems substituted for static anchors |

---

## 🟡 CARD 4 — [HIGH LEDGE] · Special Operations and Observation

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Suitable Sites** | Rooftop maintenance scaffolding · industrial facade work · high-altitude via ferrata vista points designated as observation-only · long-distance photography or survey camps |
| **Required Protection** | **Industrial sub-type:** fall-arrest system meeting EN 361 or national equivalent; hi-vis reflective vest mandatory; rope-access technician license (IRATA or equivalent) required for any commercial work on structure. **Observation sub-type:** fenced or roped viewing platform; no personal climbing rope required; binoculars and telephoto equipment permitted |
| **Minimum Entry** | Either (a) licensed rope-access technician for all engineering tasks — recreational climbing credentials are NOT interchangeable, or (b) no climbing qualification required for fenced observation positions. Recreational climbers may NOT be reassigned to industrial operations on the basis of climbing ability alone |
| **Unacceptable External Scenes** | Bare natural rock faces presented as industrial work sites · ice tools · canyon rope systems · recreational chalk bags · children in climbing harnesses unless under direct licensed supervision · natural terrain with no structure or fixed infrastructure visible |

### Why These Four Cannot Be Combined by "Height" Alone

**Reason 1 — Tools Are Not Interchangeable**
The ice climber carries axes and crampons that would be physically useless in a canyon gap and a safety liability on scaffolding. The canyon climber's static rope anchor system assumes bilateral rock walls — it cannot be installed on an open ice face or a brick parapet. The roof worker's industrial fall-arrest lanyard is rated for structural attachment points, not rock features. Assigning these images to the same card on the basis that all four persons are "high up" would require accepting that the tools are interchangeable — which they are not, and which would be dangerous to pretend.

**Reason 2 — Certification Bodies Are Legally Distinct**
- Ice wall: mountaineering federation or alpine club certification
- Canyon: canyoneering guide certification or confined-space safety training
- High-altitude natural via ferrata: recreational climbing federation
- Industrial rooftop: IRATA or national rope-access technician license

None of these qualifications are recognized as substitutes by the others. A certified ice climber is not legally authorized to perform rooftop industrial work. A rope-access technician is not qualified to lead a canyon expedition. These are not matters of difficulty — they are matters of legal liability, insurance, and regulated professional domains.

**Reason 3 — Risk Profiles Are Categorically Different**
| Image | Primary Risk | Secondary Risk | Height as Factor? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ice Wall | Ice fracture; hypothermia; tool failure | Partner loss of contact | Yes, but secondary to temperature |
| Canyon | Flooding; rockfall from both walls; anchor failure in confined space | No exit if water rises | Height is almost irrelevant; confinement is the threat |
| Natural High Rock | Exposure; weather change; no fixed protection below | Foothold failure | Yes, but the child's gear absence is the primary concern |
| Roof Scaffolding | Structural failure; industrial debris; regulatory non-compliance | Employer liability | Height matters in injury calculation, not in prevention method |

**Conclusion of Reason 3**: Height is a consequence of these environments, not the unifying factor. Each of these four risks demands a completely different prevention strategy, a different trained response, and a different piece of legislation.

**Reason 4 — The "Height" Label Would Destroy Card Specificity**
If these four images were combined under a single "High Places" card, the card would simultaneously require: ice axes, static canyon rope, industrial fall-arrest lanyard, and no special equipment (observation). This is a contradiction — a card that requires mutually exclusive equipment is not a card; it is an unregulated void.

# PART TWO — THREE SPECIFIC DETERMINATIONS

---

## Determination 1: Most Vulnerable Qualification Link — Training Wall to Natural Rock Wall

**The vulnerable link is not the skill level. It is the helmet.**

The transition from Card 1 to Card 2 crosses the Chain A-2 step (Image 3 → Image 9). Both images, taken as primary evidence, carry the same equipment deficiency: **no helmet is visibly worn or documented**.

This creates a specific structural weakness:

```
Image 3 ──[GAP]──► Image 9
No helmet          No helmet
Card 1             Card 2

The upgrade appears valid on all other grounds:
• Surface changes ✅ (artificial → natural)
• Card changes ✅ (1 → 2)
• Technique level appears to advance ✅
• Outdoor environment ✅

BUT: The one item whose absence is merely loggable in Card 1
     becomes a formal protocol violation in Card 2.

The vulnerability: A climber who was never required to wear a helmet
                   on an indoor wall arrives at a natural rock face
                   without the habit, the equipment, or the
                   documentation of wearing one.
```

**The helmet is the link because it is the first protection upgrade that must occur before the card upgrade is valid — and it is the first protection upgrade that both images fail to confirm.**

The link is not theoretical (it is not "they might fall differently outdoors"). The link is a **physical object** — the helmet — that does not appear in either transition image.

---

## Determination 2: Image Most Likely to Impersonate Formal Climbing While Only Documenting Site or Project Status

**Image 7** — Long-Distance Cliff View

```
WHY IT APPEARS TO BE FORMAL CLIMBING:

• Multiple human figures are visible on the rock face
• Those figures appear to be using ropes and equipment
• The cliff is large, impressive, and clearly used for climbing
• The image could be captioned "group rock climbing session"
  and appear credible to a non-specialist viewer

WHY IT CANNOT FUNCTION AS FORMAL CLIMBING DOCUMENTATION:

• No individual helmet is verifiable from this distance
• No individual harness is verifiable
• No anchor system is verifiable
• No belayer role is verifiable
• The photographer is not among the climbers and has no
  certifiable relationship to them
• The image documents a PLACE where climbing occurs,
  not a PERSON who is climbing at any verifiable standard

ADMINISTRATIVE DETERMINATION:

Image 7 is a site-status document. It confirms that this rock face
exists, is in use, and is of a scale appropriate for group routes.
It cannot confirm that any specific person completed any specific
climb to any specific standard.

If submitted as personal qualification evidence, it must be rejected —
not because the climbing didn't happen, but because the image
contains no personal evidence that it did.
```

**Image 4 (Rooftop Industrial Worker) and Image 2 (Ice Wall Climber)**

```
SHARED VISUAL ELEMENT:

WHY THEY CANNOT SHARE A MISSION CARD:

TOOL EXCLUSION:
Image 2's climber uses ice axes that physically
cannot penetrate brick, concrete, or metal scaffolding.
Image 4's worker uses a scaffold platform that does not
exist in any frozen environment.

SURFACE EXCLUSION:
Frozen water ice behaves fundamentally differently
under load from cut stone or brick mortar.
The fall response in each environment requires
completely different belay physics.

CERTIFICATION EXCLUSION:
Card 3 [White Fang] is issued by a mountaineering authority.
Card 4 [High Ledge] industrial sub-type is issued by a

share jurisdiction, standards, or mutual recognition agreements.

Card 3 requires a recreational extreme-sports practitioner
with wilderness emergency capability.

under employer health-and-safety legislation.
These are legally distinct roles in most national jurisdictions.

### IMAGE 1 — Belayer / Group Supervisor

**Primary Role: Executor — Active Belay**
The figure in red at the base is managing a live rope under load from at least one climber. This is an active, ongoing physical task. Their hands are on the rope; they are in stance. They are an executor of a safety-critical function.

**Alternate Role: Reviewer — Group Progression Supervisor**
If the figure at the base is also responsible for assessing each climber's technique, deciding the order of ascent, and communicating hazard calls to the group, they hold a reviewer role: evaluating performance, not merely managing rope.

**What Evidence is Needed to Switch from Executor to Reviewer?**
- A visible group session log or register in-frame or in supplementary documentation
- Evidence that the belayer is providing verbal or gestural instruction (no audio available from image)
- Documentation of their belay instructor certification, distinct from basic belay certification
- At least one other image showing them in a non-belaying supervisory position in the same session

**Note**: Both roles may be held simultaneously — but the alternate role cannot be registered as primary without the above evidence. Currently, only the belay rope is visible. The teaching relationship is absent from the image.

### IMAGE 2 — Ice Climber / Route Data Holder

**Primary Role: Executor — Active Ice Ascent**
The figure is mid-climb on a frozen surface, both axes engaged, crampons biting. This is unambiguous active execution.

**Alternate Role: Custodian — Route Data Holder**
If this person is the first to ascend this specific ice formation, or if they are conducting a route assessment to determine whether this line is safe for other guild members, they hold a custodian role — they are not climbing for personal advancement but to generate data about the route itself.

**What Evidence is Needed to Switch from Executor to Custodian?**
- A route-assessment sheet, GPS record, or written report connecting this image to a formal route survey
- Identification of the ice formation as a previously unregistered or seasonal route
- Documentation confirming the climb was conducted under a route-survey commission, not a personal advancement session
- Visible presence of a camera mount or data-recording device on gear — none is currently visible

**Primary Role: Executor — Rooftop Industrial Task**
The worker is actively performing a physical task on a brick parapet. Their body position (leaning over the edge, braced on scaffold) confirms active work, not inspection.

**Alternate Role: Custodian — Site Compliance Witness**
If the worker is inspecting the scaffold or parapet condition prior to a larger operation, rather than performing the final task, their role shifts from executor to custodian — they are preserving the integrity of the worksite for subsequent operatives.

**What Evidence is Needed to Switch from Executor to Custodian?**

### IMAGE 6 — Unregistered Participant / Suspended Executor Candidate

**Primary Role: Bystander — Unregistered Participant**
In the absence of harness, helmet, rope, or adult partner documentation, the child can only be registered as a bystander at an uncontrolled high-altitude location. This is not a dismissal — it is a holding state.

**Alternate Role: Executor — Via Ferrata Candidate (Suspended)**
If all five visual evidence conditions from Volume I are met, the child transitions from bystander to executor on a registered via ferrata route. This is the most complete role transition available within the system.

**What Evidence is Needed to Switch from Bystander to Executor?**
Exactly the five items documented in Volume I, restated here as role conditions:
1. A fitted harness (object — not present in image)
2. A certified adult partner in-frame or in supplementary documentation (person — not present)
3. Named via ferrata route registration confirming the iron rung is part of a fixed cable system (place — not confirmed)
4. Climbing helmet meeting impact standards (object — not present)
5. A rope or via ferrata lanyard connecting climber to route at any point (object — not present)

**Until all five are met, the role remains Bystander.** The alternate role of Executor exists in the card system as a possibility, not a status.

---

### IMAGE 7 — Site Recorder / Uninvolved Bystander

**Primary Role: Recorder — Site Documentation**
The photographer has produced a record of a climbing site in active use. This is a recording action: the image captures the state of the environment at a moment in time. The recorder role is valid.

**Alternate Role: Bystander — Uninvolved Observer**
If the photographer has no relationship to the climbers visible on the cliff — no shared session log, no commission from the guild, no designated survey role — then they are simply a bystander who happened to photograph a cliff. The image's evidential value collapses to near zero for guild purposes.

**What Evidence is Needed to Confirm Recorder Over Bystander?**
- A guild commission authorizing the photography of this site
- A session log connecting the photographer to the climbing party visible in the image
- A caption, date stamp, or location record confirming this was a deliberate documentation visit
- Any supplementary image showing the photographer's position relative to the climbers (a bystander on a hiking trail and a designated guild recorder may occupy the same physical position)

---

## Selected Combination

```
Image 8 → Image 3 → Image 9 → Image 10
[Inflatable]  [Indoor]   [Sport Rock]  [Trad Night]
Card 1 Sub    Card 1     Card 2 Entry  Card 2 Ceiling
```

**This chain appears continuous.** Each step advances logically. Each image builds on the previous one. A reader tracing this chain would naturally conclude they are looking at one person's complete development from absolute beginner to advanced trad climber.

**The chain is not continuous.**

---

## What Is Missing — Audit by Category

> **Audit Rule: What is missing must be named as a specific object, action, place, or condition absent from the images. It may not be described as common sense, assumed knowledge, or background fact. It must be something that does not appear anywhere in the four images.**

---

### Missing OBJECT 1: The First Piece of Traditional Protection

Between Image 9 and Image 10, a fundamental equipment transition occurs. Image 9 shows a climber clipping or holding onto natural rock features without placing any gear. Image 10 shows a climber wearing a full rack of cams, nuts, and slings.

**The object that is missing**: **A cam or nut being placed into a crack in rock.**

Across all four images in the chain, this physical action — inserting a piece of removable protection into a rock feature — **never appears**. Not in any image. Not partially, not in preparation, not after the fact. The rack in Image 10 appears as if it arrived fully loaded on the climber's harness without any intermediate step showing how it came to be used.

This is not common sense (everyone knows you have to practice placing gear). This is a **specific physical action involving a specific object that is entirely absent from the visual record**.

---

### Missing ACTION 2: The Anchor Being Built

Between Image 3 (indoor wall, top-rope attached to pre-set anchor) and Image 9 (outdoor sport route, pre-set bolt anchor), and continuing to Image 10 (trad traverse, self-placed anchor system), the act of **building an anchor** never appears.

**The action that is missing**: **A climber's hands connecting two or more pieces of protection to a single load-bearing point using a sling, cord, or rope.**

An anchor is the foundational safety structure of all non-beginner climbing. It appears in the chain's outcome (Image 10 is alive, therefore anchors exist) but never in the process. The chain documents the climber before anchors and after anchors but contains no image of anchors being built.

This is not common sense. This is a **specific physical action — hands on cord, cord through gear, cord tied to station — that does not appear anywhere in these four images**.

---

### Missing PLACE 3: An Intermediate Outdoor Slab or Easy Crag

Between Image 3 (indoor wall) and Image 9 (advanced sport route on steep natural stone), there should be a location: a low-angle outdoor slab, an easy beginner crag, an introductory outdoor site where the transition from controlled artificial surface to live natural rock occurs.

**The place that is missing**: **A low-angle natural rock face, probably granite or sandstone, with visible easy angle (less than 70 degrees), showing a beginner-level outdoor session.**

This is not an assumed step. It is a **specific terrain type — a gentle outdoor slab — that appears nowhere in the four images**. Image 9 immediately presents a steep, technical face. No gradual outdoor transition surface exists in the visual record of this chain. The climber appears to have teleported from an indoor wall to a steep sport route without any image of the intermediate terrain.

---

### Missing CONDITION 4: Daylight on Image 10's Route

Image 10 shows a low-light or near-darkness condition confirmed by the active headlamp. The preceding three images — inflatable wall (daylight, outdoor event), indoor wall (interior lighting), sport route (daylight, outdoor) — all take place in adequate or controlled light.

**The condition that is missing**: **A prior session log entry, a date-time stamp, or a supplementary image confirming that Image 10's climber has completed at least one documented night or low-light climb before this traverse.**

The headlamp being activated means this is a deliberate night operation. Night operations have separate requirements in Card 2. Yet the chain contains no image showing the climber in any **prior low-light condition**. This is not about whether they have done it before — this is about the specific visual condition of **reduced ambient light affecting visibility** being documented at an earlier stage, which it is not.

# PREAMBLE — TRIBUNAL PROCEDURE

All appeals are evaluated against the card definitions, level boundaries, and card replacement conditions established in Volume I and confirmed in Volume II. The Tribunal may issue three verdicts:

| Verdict | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **APPROVED** | Appeal accepted as submitted; card relationship updated accordingly |
| **DOWNGRADED** | Appeal partially accepted; a restricted version is registered with named conditions |
| **REJECTED** | Appeal denied; original registration stands; substitution in the applied direction is prohibited |

Each ruling must cite at least one ground from: site nature · protection method · character recognizability · technical threshold · mission purpose.

A minimum revised version is provided for all cases where a single condition change could save the appeal.

# APPEAL A
## Application: Reclassify Image 04 (Rooftop Industrial Worker) as an Exterior Wall Climbing Task under Card 2 [IRON FIST]

---

### Tribunal Analysis

**Applicant's Presumed Argument:**
The worker is on an exterior wall surface, is elevated, is using physical effort to maintain position, and is working on the face of a building — all of which superficially resemble exterior rock climbing.

**Ground 1 — Site Nature: FAILS**

```
Card 2 [IRON FIST] designates:
"Outdoor sport-climbing crags · trad routes · sequential group-route
cliffs · via ferrata fixed-line ridges · boulder fields with crash pads"

Image 4 site is:
Brick parapet atop a multi-storey urban building in an active
construction or maintenance zone, surrounded by scaffolding frames,
with a city skyline as the primary backdrop.

A brick parapet is not a crag.
A scaffold frame is not a via ferrata fixed line.
A construction zone is not a boulder field.

These are not approximate mismatches — they are categorically
different physical environments governed by different physics,
different anchor points, and different hazard profiles.
```

**Ground 2 — Protection Method: FAILS**

```
Card 2 requires:
Helmet + harness + lead rope or top-rope anchored to natural or
fixed protection + certified belayer.

Image 4 shows:
Hard hat (construction grade, not climbing grade) · hi-vis vest ·
scaffold platform as primary work surface · NO visible climbing
rope · NO visible harness · NO visible belayer.

The worker is not protected by a climbing system.
If they are protected at all, it is by an industrial fall-arrest
lanyard rated for scaffold attachment — a legally distinct device.
Substituting industrial fall-arrest for climbing rope protection
would violate both systems simultaneously.
```

**Ground 3 — Mission Purpose: FAILS**

```
Card 2 mission purpose: recreational skill advancement,
route completion, or supervised training on natural terrain.

Image 4 mission purpose: completion of a commercial construction
or maintenance task on a client's property under employer
occupational health and safety obligations.

These purposes are not interchangeable. A climber completing
a sport route has no employer, no client property liability,
and no regulatory duty of care to a third party. An industrial
operative has all three. Merging these mission purposes would
expose the guild to legal liability for work it did not commission
and cannot supervise.
```

**Ground 4 — Character Recognizability: FAILS**

```
The individual in Image 4 is identifiable as an industrial
operative by four visible markers:
(1) Hi-vis reflective vest — mandatory in active construction zones
(2) Construction-grade hard hat — distinct from climbing helmet
(3) Scaffold platform — no equivalent in climbing environments
(4) Brick parapet — no equivalent in any climbing card's site list

These markers are not incidental to the image.
They are the primary identification system.
Reclassifying this person as a climber requires erasing all four markers —
which means reclassifying the image, not interpreting it.
```

---

### VERDICT: ❌ REJECTED

**Rejection is total.** No partial registration within Card 2 is possible for this image under any framing of "exterior wall climbing" because the site, protection method, mission purpose, and character identification all fail independently. The failure is not marginal — each ground is individually sufficient to reject the appeal.

---

### Minimum Revised Version

> The only scenario in which this image could approach a Card 2 relationship is if the entire context of the image were changed — and at that point, it would be a different image.
>
> However, if the appeal is reframed as:
> *"Retain Image 4 in Card 4 Industrial, and create a separate Side-by-Side Display Note pairing it with a Card 2 image to contrast industrial versus recreational exterior wall work"*
>
> — then this reframing is **approved within Tier B (Same-Shelf Display)** under the mandatory separation footnote protocol established in Volume II.
>
> **This is not a reclassification. It is a display permission only.**

---

### Mutually Exclusive Tag — Appeal A

| Tag | Card 2 [IRON FIST] | Card 4 Industrial [HIGH LEDGE] | Cannot Be Shared Because |
|---|---|---|---|
| **"Employer occupational liability applies to this activity"** | ✗ Never | ✅ Always | Recreational climbing has no employer-employee legal relationship; the moment this tag applies, the activity exits recreational card jurisdiction entirely |
| **"Hi-vis vest worn by the operative"** | ✗ Disqualifying | ✅ Mandatory | Hi-vis vests signal regulatory inspection zones; their presence on a rock face would indicate a mislabeled scene, not a new card tier |
| **"Scaffold frame as primary platform"** | ✗ Incompatible | ✅ Defining | Scaffold frames are manufactured infrastructure; Card 2 requires natural or purpose-built recreational terrain — these are mutually exclusive surface types |

## Application: Use Image 07 (Distant Cliff View) as Action Proof for Image 09 (Sport Climber on Natural Rock)

---

### Tribunal Analysis

**Applicant's Presumed Argument:**

A climber executing a strenuous crimp sequence on

# APPEAL E
## Application: Merge Image 05 (Canyon Crevice) and Image 10 (Trad Night Traverse) into the Same Natural Rock Wall High-Risk Task

---

### Tribunal Analysis

**Applicant's Presumed Argument:**
Both images show highly experienced climbers in demanding conditions on rock surfaces. Both involve sophisticated rope systems and serious risk management. Combining them under a "Natural Rock Wall High-Risk" category would create a unified advanced tier.

**Ground 1 — Site Nature: FAILS**

```
Image 5 site:
A canyon crevice — a narrow slot formed by two converging
rock walls pressing on the climber's body simultaneously.
The defining geometric feature is bilateral confinement.
The climber cannot fall freely — they are pressed between
two walls. The rope anchor is horizontal or diagonal to
the canyon axis, not vertical as in open climbing.

Image 10 site:
An open rock face — the climber traverses horizontally
across a surface with free exposure on the downhill side.
The defining geometric feature is single-surface exposure.
The climber can fall in a predictable arc governed by
the rope's attachment point.

These are not variations of the same environment.
They are geometrically opposite risk geometries:
• Canyon: confined bilateral · fall is constrained
• Open traverse: single surface · fall is open-arc

Rope physics, anchor placement, and emergency extraction
all differ fundamentally between these two geometries.
```

**Ground 2 — Protection Method: FAILS**

```
Image 5 protection:
Static white rope anchored above canyon entry point ·
rope runs diagonally through the crevice ·
anchor must grip bilateral rock surfaces or a
feature at the canyon top · no bolt anchors typically
available in canyon terrain

Image 10 protection:
Dynamic climbing rope (implied by gear rack) ·
trad protection placed by the climber into
horizontal or vertical rock features ·
multi-directional anchor loading ·
open-face fall trajectory management

These protection systems are not interchangeable:
• Static rope in canyon context ≠ dynamic rope on face
• Canyon anchor physics ≠ open-face anchor physics
• A trad climber's placed gear would not function as
  a canyon anchor in a crevice geometry
• A canyon static rope would be inappropriate as a
  dynamic belay device on an open face
```

**Ground 3 — Card Boundary: FAILS BY CARD DEFINITION**

```
Image 5: Card 3 [WHITE FANG] — Canyon Sub-type
Image 10: Card 2 [IRON FIST] — Advanced Trad Sub-type
          (at the threshold of Card 3, but not yet Card 3)

These are different cards.
Merging them would require either:
(a) Demoting Image 10 to Card 3 without evidence of
    canyon or ice environment experience — invalid
(b) Promoting Image 5's canyon environment to
    Card 2 natural rock — invalid, as canyon geometry
    exceeds Card 2's site definition

More critically: Image 10 is at the Card 2 ceiling.
It has not been granted Card 3 status.
Card 3 status requires an environment-specific course
that does not appear in Image 10's current record.
Merging it with a Card 3 image would effectively
grant Card 3 status without the required evidence —
bypassing the very certification the card system exists to enforce.
```

**Ground 4 — Mission Purpose: FAILS**

```
Image 5 mission purpose:
Navigation of a confined geological feature requiring
canyon-specific rope management and emergency awareness
(flooding, rockfall from bilateral walls, entrapment risk).

Image 10 mission purpose:
Technical rock climbing featuring self-placed protection,
route-finding on complex terrain, and extended duration
in low-light conditions.

"Natural Rock Wall High-Risk" would collapse the
distinction between these two mission purposes into
a single category defined only by difficulty.

Difficulty is not a category.
Difficulty is an attribute that applies differently
in different environments.

A grade-5 canyon difficulty involves hydraulic entrapment risk.
A grade-5 open-face difficulty involves fall-arc management.
These require different training, different gear, and
different emergency responses.
Combining them under "high-risk" erases the information
the card system was designed to preserve.
```

---

### VERDICT: ❌ REJECTED

**The merger fails on all four grounds independently.** Most critically, it would grant Image 10 Card 3 status without evidence of the required environment-specific course, and it would grant Image 5's canyon sub-type the open-face protection framework of Card 2 — both of which represent false qualification records.

The appeal's premise — that "high-risk" is a valid card category — is itself rejected. High-risk is an attribute. It cannot be a card definition.

---

### Minimum Revised Version

> The appeal cannot be saved by changing one condition because it conflates two structurally incompatible environments. However, the closest valid version is:
>
> **Revised Application:** *"Register Image 5 and Image 10 as a Side-by-Side Display pair under the Title 'Advanced Experience — Parallel High-Risk Environments,' with a mandatory footnote confirming they inhabit different cards, require different protection systems, and cannot be used interchangeably as qualification evidence for either environment."*
>
> This is **approved within Tier B (Same-Shelf Display)** with the following footnote:
>
> *"Image 5 (Card 3 Canyon) and Image 10 (Card 2 Ceiling / Card 3 Threshold) are displayed together to demonstrate that advanced climbing experience takes non-equivalent forms in different terrain types. They share: high technical demand · full safety gear · solitary operation requiring self-sufficiency. They do not share: site geometry · protection method · card classification · applicable certification. Neither image may be used as qualification evidence for the other's environment."*

> What is needed: A documented moment in which the same individual **transfers from the climbing role to the belaying role** — either within a single session (finishing a climb, then taking the rope and setting up belay) or across two sessions (final climbing session log entry followed by first belaying session log entry on the same logbook page).
>
> This action — the role transition — does not appear in either image. Image 3 shows climbing; Image 1 shows belaying. The intermediate moment where climbing ends and teaching begins has no visual or documentary record.
>
> **The missing action is: a role transition event, documented either visually (person handing rope to belayer / person receiving rope as new belayer) or in a session log entry dated between Image 3 and Image 1.**

---

**Missing Place 3: An Outdoor Transition Location**

> What is needed: An image or session log entry documenting that the same individual **was physically present at an outdoor natural rock face at any point** between the indoor training wall session (Image 3) and the group belaying session (Image 1).
>
> Image 3 takes place indoors. Image 1 takes place outdoors on natural rock. The gap between them contains no documented outdoor visit. A person who has never been outdoors on natural rock before the day they belay a group on a natural rock face has no applicable site-hazard knowledge for that environment.
>
> **The missing place is: any outdoor natural rock location — even a beginner-level slab — documented between the two images.**

---

**Missing Condition 4: Identity Confirmation Across Both Images**

> What is needed: A documentary record confirming that **the same person appears in both images** — a registration form, a session log with matching names, a dated series of photographs, or any document that links a specific individual to both Image 3's training session and Image 1's belaying session.
>
> Currently, Image 3 shows a child of approximately 8–10 years old. Image 1 shows an adult or older teenager. These could be the same person five or more years apart. They could be different people entirely. Neither image contains any identifying information that connects them.
>
> **The missing condition is: any documentary confirmation that a specific named individual appears in both sessions.**

---

### Why This Record Is Retained Rather Than Rejected

> This record is retained — rather than rejected outright — for three reasons:
>
> **Reason 1:** The narrative direction (trainee → instructor) is a valid and guild-recognized progression. The arc is not false; only the evidence is incomplete.
>
> **Reason 2:** The missing evidence is collectable. Unlike Appeal C (where the missing evidence is an entire card tier that cannot be retroactively created) or Appeal B (where the missing evidence is physically impossible to produce from a landscape photograph), Appeal D's missing evidence consists of normal session documentation that a real person would ordinarily generate.
>
> **Reason 3:** The illustrative value of this chain — as an educational display showing what progression looks like — is genuine. Rejecting it entirely would deprive the guild of a useful teaching tool. Retaining it as an illustration, while refusing to grant it qualification status, preserves both values.
>
> **The record is retained for now** because it represents a real possibility in a temporary state of insufficient evidence — which is different from a false claim or an impossible substitution.

# SECTION FIVE — GENERAL GUILD LAW

## When Is a Climbing Image Enough to Upgrade? When Is It Just Proof That Everyone Is High Up?

---

## ARTICLE I — THE UPGRADE THRESHOLD

A climbing image is sufficient to support a card upgrade **only when all five of the following conditions are simultaneously present in the image or its directly attached supplementary documentation:**

---

### Condition 1 — A Specific Individual Is Identifiable

> The image must contain a person whose identity can be connected to a qualification record. "Connected" means: a session log entry with the same date and location, a registration form with the person's name, or a guild-issued identifier visible in the frame.
>
> A person whose face is turned away but whose gear configuration is documented is marginally acceptable if the gear is documented as personally owned or guild-issued. A person who is one of many figures on a cliff face and who cannot be individually resolved from the background is not identifiable by any standard.
>
> **An image without an identifiable individual can never upgrade anyone.**

---

### Condition 2 — The Protection System Is Fully Visible

> The image must show the protection system actively in use, not merely present. "Active" means: the rope is under tension, the harness is being loaded, the anchor is bearing weight, the belay device is engaged.
>
> A rope lying on the ground next to a climber is not protection in use. A harness hanging on a peg is not protection in use. A helmet attached to a bag is not protection in use.
>
> **An image where the protection exists but is not actively deployed cannot confirm that the climber was protected during the climb.**

---

### Condition 3 — The Site Is Positively Identified as Matching the Card Definition

> The image must show a site that matches the card's designated site type. Natural rock face for Card 2. Ice formation for Card 3 ice sub-type. Bilateral canyon walls for Card 3 canyon sub-type. Artificial manufactured surface for Card 1.
>
> A site that is merely "rocky" does not confirm Card 2. A site that is merely "cold" does not confirm Card 3 ice. A site that is merely "narrow" does not confirm Card 3 canyon. The site type must be positively identifiable from the image's visible features.
>
> **An image where the site is ambiguous, partially visible, or distant cannot confirm card-specific site qualification.**

---

### Condition 4 — The Technical Threshold Is Assessable

> The image must show enough of the climber's body, gear, and immediate environment to allow a qualified reviewer to assess whether the technical demands of the activity are consistent with the card being claimed.
>
> For Card 2: grip type, foot placement, rope angle, and body tension must be assessable. For Card 3: tool deployment, environmental exposure, and anchor physics must be assessable. For Card 1: harness fit and rope attachment must be assessable.
>
> **An image where the technical action is obscured, distant, or incomplete cannot confirm technical threshold compliance.**

---

### Condition 5 — The Mission Purpose Is Consistent with the Card's Designated Purpose

> The image must show activity consistent with the card's defined mission purpose. Recreational skill advancement or route completion for Card 2. Extreme environment navigation for Card 3. Industrial regulated work for Card 4. Beginner training for Card 1.
>
> An industrial worker at height is not performing a Card 2 recreational mission. A landscape photographer on a hilltop is not performing a Card 3 extreme environment mission. A child on a carnival ride is not performing a Card 1 formal training mission unless the specific conditions of Card 1 are met.
>
> **An image whose mission purpose belongs to a different card cannot be reclassified by the difficulty or height of the activity shown.**

---

## ARTICLE II — THE "EVERYONE IS HIGH UP" FAILURE MODE

An image fails to qualify as upgrade evidence — and must instead be classified as site documentation, engineering operations record, or observation evidence — when it meets any of the following conditions:

---

### Failure Mode 1 — Height Is the Only Shared Feature

> If the only thing connecting two images is that both show people above the ground, those images share nothing that the guild recognizes as a qualification criterion. Height is a consequence of climbing. It is not climbing. A construction worker, an ice climber, a canyon navigator, and a child on a ridge may all be ten meters above the ground simultaneously, but they are not performing the same activity, they are not protected by the same system, and they do not hold the same qualifications.
>
> **When height is the argument, the argument has failed.**

---

### Failure Mode 2 — The Individual Cannot Be Separated from the Background

> If the person whose qualification is being claimed cannot be individually identified — because they are too distant, because they are one of many similar figures, because their back is turned and their gear is unreadable — then the image documents a scene, not a person.
>
> Scene documentation belongs in the Observation sub-type or the Long-Range Circumstantial Evidence column. It does not belong in any personal qualification record.
>
> **When the person disappears into the landscape, the upgrade disappears with them.**

---

### Failure Mode 3 — The Tool or Protection System Belongs to a Different Card

> If the most prominent piece of equipment in the image belongs to a different card's required protection system — industrial fall-arrest lanyard in a climbing context, ice axes on a manufactured wall, recreational chalk bag on a scaffold — the image is misassigned regardless of who is using the equipment or how skilled they appear.
>
> Equipment identifies card type. The wrong equipment disqualifies the card claim before any other assessment is made.
>
> **When the tool belongs to a different card, the image belongs to a different card.**

---

### Failure Mode 4 — The Site Precludes the Card Being Claimed

> If the site visible in the image is definitively incompatible with the card being claimed — an urban skyline behind a claimed Card 2 natural-rock scene, a manufactured surface beneath a claimed Card 3 extreme-environment ascent — the site disqualifies the claim regardless of the climber's apparent skill.
>
> A skilled trad climber photographed on an indoor training wall is not performing a Card 2 mission. A beginner photographed on a glacier is not performing a Card 3 mission. The site determines the card type before the skill level is assessed.
>
> **When the site is wrong, the card is wrong.**

---

### Failure Mode 5 — The Image Documents a Process Stage, Not a Qualification Achievement

> If the image shows preparation, rest, inspection, observation, or approach — rather than active climbing with an active protection system — it documents a process stage, not a climbing achievement.
>
> A climber looking at a route from the base is not climbing the route. A belayer waiting for the climber to begin is not belaying. A person standing at the top of a cliff looking at the view is not performing the climb that brought them there.
>
> **When the action has not started or has already ended, the qualification cannot be confirmed.**

---

## ARTICLE III — THE GENERAL RULE, STATED PLAINLY

```
A climbing image is enough to upgrade when:
It shows a specific person, actively protected,
on a correctly identified site, performing an assessable
technical action, for a purpose consistent with the
card being claimed.

A climbing image is only proof that everyone is high up when:
It shows height without identity, or protection without
deployment, or a site without specificity, or action
without assessability, or purpose without card alignment.

The difference is not how impressive the image looks.
The difference is how much of the card definition
the image can confirm — one condition at a time,
without inference, without assumption, and without
substituting visual drama for documentary evidence.
```

---

## ARTICLE IV — THE THREE IMAGES THAT MOST CLEARLY DEMONSTRATE THIS LAW

**Image 7 demonstrates Failure Mode 2:**
A visually striking cliff face covered in climbers, none of whom can be individually identified. The image is compelling. It is evidentially empty for any personal qualification purpose. It belongs in Long-Range Circumstantial Evidence, not in any personal record.

**Image 4 demonstrates Failure Mode 3 and 4:**
A person at height using equipment that belongs to a different regulatory domain. The height is real. The effort is real. The qualification — for any climbing card — is absent. The tool (industrial equipment) and the site (urban scaffolding) both disqualify the climbing-card claim before the climber's skill is assessed.

**Image 6 demonstrates Failure Mode 5 and the upgrade suspension:**
A person at height performing what might be climbing or might be unprotected scrambling, using what might be a via ferrata rung or might be a coincidental rural fixture, wearing no gear that can be confirmed as climbing-appropriate. The height is real. The boldness is real. The record is suspended. It will remain suspended until five specific missing objects, actions, places, and conditions are supplied — not because the guild doubts what happened, but because the guild cannot confirm what happened from what is visible.

---

## CLOSING STATEMENT OF THE FINAL BOOK

```
The Aka Rope Guild registers climbing missions.
It does not register height.
It does not register bravery.
It does not register impressive landscapes.
It does not register industrial operations.
It does not register children at viewpoints.
It does not register photographers on hiking trails.

It registers specific people, with specific tools,
in specific places, performing specific actions,
at specific levels of verified qualification.

When an image shows all of these things, it belongs
in the card column that matches its conditions.

When an image shows only some of these things, it belongs
in a holding state, an annotation role, or a side-by-side
display position — pending the evidence that would make it whole.

When an image shows none of these things except height,
it belongs nowhere in the upgrade chain.
It belongs, at most, in the observation column —
as proof that high places exist,
and that people sometimes go to them,
and that the guild cannot tell, from this image alone,
whether those people were climbing or merely standing.

Both are real.
Only one qualifies.
```

## PART THREE: THE SIX-STEP UPGRADE CHAIN — NEWBIE TO ROCK WALL

---

```
STEP 1 ──► STEP 2 ──► STEP 3 ──► STEP 4 ──► STEP 5 ──► STEP 6

### STEP 1: "First Touch"
**Evidence image:** Photograph 8 (inflatable wall, child, white helmet)
**Card:** A — Stone Skin Initiation (inflatable variant)
**Status:** ⚠️ CIRCUMSTANTIAL EVIDENCE ONLY — not a true upgrade step

*Reason:* The inflatable surface does not build genuine rock-reading skills. The coloured handholds are oversized and sequenced for guidance. This step proves only that the climber is willing to leave the ground and can tolerate a harness. It cannot be used as a standalone qualification — it must be paired with Step 2 before any guild stamp is issued.

### STEP 2: "Panel Grip"
**Evidence image:** Photograph 3 (rigid artificial wall, girl, blue harness)
**Card:** A — Stone Skin Initiation (rigid panel)
**Status:** ✅ REAL UPGRADE — first genuine qualification step

*Reason:* The rigid panel wall introduces fixed hold friction, weight distribution, and the experience of a static rope under tension. The transition from Step 1 to Step 2 is the first real upgrade because the surface begins to approximate actual rock texture. However: the missing helmet in Photograph 3 means this specific image cannot be stamped — a compliant re-documentation is required.

---

### STEP 3: "Supervised Crag"
**Evidence image:** Photograph 1 (group on natural rock, red rope, belayer below)
**Card:** B — Grey Face Field Test (group supervised)
**Status:** ✅ REAL UPGRADE — first outdoor natural rock experience

*Reason:* The transition from artificial panel to natural rock is the most significant perceptual shift in the entire chain. Natural rock has no colour-coded holds, no pre-planned sequence, and unpredictable texture changes. The group format with a dedicated belayer at the base is the correct first exposure. This is a genuine upgrade because the risk profile, decision-making demand, and physical reading of the surface all increase qualitatively.

---

### STEP 4: "Independent Route"
**Evidence image:** Photograph 9 (solo male, crimp hold, blue rope, close-up)
**Card:** B — Grey Face Field Test (high-difficulty, independent)
**Status:** ✅ REAL UPGRADE — transition from supervised group to independent technical climbing

*Reason:* The climber is now reading micro-features (fingertip crimps), trusting their own body positioning without a group around them, and working at a difficulty level that requires trained finger strength. The step up from Step 3 is genuine because the social safety net has been removed and the technical demand has increased substantially.

---

### STEP 5: "Committed Ascent"
**Evidence image:** Photograph 10 (female, full rack, headlamp, night or low light)
**Card:** B — Grey Face Field Test (advanced, self-placed protection)
**Status:** ✅ REAL UPGRADE — transition from sport bolt clipping to traditional self-placed gear

*Reason:* The full rack of cams and nuts visible on Photograph 10 means the climber is now responsible for creating their own protection system rather than relying on pre-existing bolts. The headlamp indicates low-light or night conditions, adding a navigation and judgment layer. This is a genuine upgrade because failure at this step is not recovered by a coach standing below — it is recovered only by the climber's own competence.

---

### STEP 6: "Distant Cliff Witness"
**Evidence image:** Photograph 7 (distant cliff face, multiple climbers, forest)
**Card:** B — Grey Face Field Test (site documentation)
**Status:** ⚠️ CIRCUMSTANTIAL EVIDENCE ONLY — not a personal upgrade, but a scale marker

*Reason:* Step 6 is not an upgrade of the individual climber — it is an upgrade of understanding. Seeing the cliff from a distance for the first time reveals the true scale of what the preceding steps have been building toward. The tiny figures on the rock face show that even at Step 5, a climber is still a small element in a much larger vertical landscape. This image cannot be used to stamp a personal qualification but is formally displayed at the end of the upgrade chain as a scale reference and motivation document.

## PART FOUR: THE HIGH-RISK PARALLEL CHAIN — NON-UPGRADEABLE BUT DISPLAYABLE SIDE BY SIDE

---

### Why These Four Cannot Be Combined by "Height" Alone

The following four scenarios all involve significant height and all involve some form of rope or safety system. They are sometimes mistakenly grouped together in casual climbing conversation. The Red Rope Guild formally prohibits this grouping for the following structural reasons:

---

**NODE A: Ice Wall** (Photograph 2)
**NODE B: Canyon Crevice** (Photograph 5)
**NODE C: Natural Outer Rock with Panoramic Exposure** (Photograph 6)
**NODE D: Industrial Rooftop / Scaffold Operation** (Photograph 4)

---

#### REASON 1: The Nature of the Hazard Is Categorically Different

| Scenario | Primary Hazard | Secondary Hazard | Recovery Method |
|----------|---------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Ice Wall | Ice fracture, tool failure, sudden temperature change | Hypothermia, crampon slip | Ice screw re-placement, partner haul |
| Canyon Crevice | Entrapment, rockfall from both walls, flooding | Claustrophobia-induced panic | Static rope ascent, partner from above |
| Open Rock Panoramic | Unprotected fall, loose rock, no anchor system confirmed | Youth exposure without harness | Via ferrata lanyard, fixed cable |
| Industrial Rooftop | Structural failure of scaffold, no dynamic belay | Non-climbing footwear, no dynamic rope | Occupational safety rescue, not guild protocol |

Height is only the common visual feature. The **type of failure**, the **recovery protocol**, and the **equipment system** are entirely different. A climber trained to survive an ice wall event (ice fracture requiring screw replacement) has no applicable skill for a scaffold collapse. A canyon crevice specialist trained for entrapment extraction has no applicable skill for open exposure on an unanchored rocky slope.

---

#### REASON 2: The Rope Systems Are Incompatible

- **Ice Wall** uses a dynamic rope running through ice screws — the system is designed to absorb the shock of a fall by stretching.
- **Canyon Crevice** uses a static or semi-static rope for controlled lowering and ascending — a dynamic rope would behave dangerously in a chimney rappel.
- **Open Rocky Panoramic** shows a fixed iron cable — this is neither a dynamic nor a static rope, it is fixed infrastructure; using a climbing rope system here would require a via ferrata-specific energy-absorbing lanyard.
- **Industrial Rooftop** shows no rope system at all that meets guild standards — the scaffold is a structural support, not a belay system.

Grouping these by "all use ropes" or "all involve height" is therefore technically false for at least two of the four cases, and misleading for all four.

---

#### REASON 3: The Climber's Orientation to the Environment Is Different

- On an **ice wall**, the climber faces the surface and actively strikes it.
- In a **canyon crevice**, the climber is surrounded by the surface on multiple sides simultaneously and uses pressure rather than striking.
- On an **open rocky panoramic**, the climber is moving across a surface with a valley drop below — the psychological orientation is outward toward open space.
- On an **industrial rooftop**, the worker faces a brick wall but is operating on a constructed surface that was never designed to be climbed — the entire relationship between body and surface is tool-based, not movement-based.

---

#### FORMAL PROHIBITION STATEMENT

> *The Red Rope Guild formally records that height in metres is not a valid common denominator for mission card classification. Two climbers at 50 metres elevation, one on ice and one in a canyon, face environments so structurally different that shared training is not possible, shared equipment is not safe, and shared emergency response is not applicable. The industrial rooftop worker at 10 metres faces a greater legal and procedural incompatibility with the guild system than an ice climber at 200 metres. The open panoramic via ferrata child, though at high altitude with beautiful views, may be in greater unmitigated danger than a canyon crevice climber with a helmet and a static rope at 5 metres.*
