The physical result is a connection that **looks tight but behaves electrically as a loose connection**: the contact interface has microscopic gaps and irregular pressure distribution. By basic physics, resistance at the interface is elevated. When current flows through elevated resistance, heat is generated at that point — disproportionately and locally. At 20–48A continuous charging current, even a small increase in contact resistance generates significant localized heat. This heat further oxidizes the copper surface, further increasing resistance, generating more heat — a self-reinforcing thermal runaway loop that is invisible externally until it manifests as insulation melting, carbonization, or fire.

## Least Advisable Turning Direction: Port

Rule 19 (page 4) states explicitly:

> "Unless you are overtaking, avoid if at all possible altering your course to **port**; whenever possible alter course to **starboard**."

Since you cannot clearly classify your situation as overtaking, the default restricted-visibility guidance applies: a turn to port is the least advisable action.

## Why the Crossing Give-Way Rule Cannot Solely Determine This

The crossing rule (Rule 15, page 1) requires you to identify that the other vessel is on your **starboard side** and then keep out of her way—but this rule operates within a framework that presupposes **vessels in sight of one another**. Two critical problems arise in fog:

1. **Visibility condition not met.** The give-way/stand-on construct of Rules 13–17 applies only when vessels can see each other. In restricted visibility, Rule 19 supersedes that construct entirely. There is no "stand-on" or "give-way" vessel assignment in fog.

2. **Geometry cannot be confirmed.** Without visual contact you cannot reliably determine the other vessel's heading or aspect. You may detect a radar target forward of your beam, but you cannot confirm whether the encounter is head-on, crossing, or a borderline overtaking situation. The normal crossing rule depends on knowing the precise relative geometry—information that radar alone may not conclusively provide.

Rule 19 therefore replaces the situational give-way logic with a **universal precautionary directive**: regardless of which side the contact is on, favor a starboard turn (which in most geometries opens CPA) and avoid a port turn (which could swing your bow into the other vessel's track). This blanket guidance exists precisely because the fine distinctions of head-on versus crossing versus overtaking cannot be reliably made without sight.

# Turning Direction to Avoid in Restricted Visibility: Port is Least Advisable

## The Rule's Guidance

According to the **Conduct of Vessels in Restricted Visibility (Rule 19)** on page 4:

> *"If you detect by radar another vessel forward of your beam, take avoiding action in ample time. Unless you are overtaking, avoid if at all possible altering your course to port; whenever possible alter course to starboard."*

Therefore, **altering course to port is the least advisable** turning direction when you detect a vessel forward of your beam in fog and you are not overtaking.

## Why the Crossing Give-Way Rule Cannot Be Applied on Its Own

The usual **crossing situation rule (Rules 15 and 17)** from page 1 states that when two power-driven vessels are crossing, the vessel that has the other on her **starboard side** must give way — and the standard give-way maneuver in clear visibility is often to alter course to starboard or slow down, depending on the geometry. This rule, together with the head-on rule (both alter to starboard for port-to-port passage), provides clear guidance **when vessels are in sight of one another**.

However, in restricted visibility:

1. **You cannot visually classify the encounter.** The quick-reference diagrams for head-on, crossing, and overtaking on page 1 all depend on **seeing** the aspect of the other vessel — its relative bearing, heading, and which side you are viewing. In fog, with only a radar contact forward of your beam, you **cannot reliably determine** whether the situation is head-on, crossing-from-starboard, or crossing-from-port.

2. **The maneuvering signals do not apply.** Page 4 explicitly states that short-blast warning and maneuvering signals (one blast for starboard, two for port) are *"only sounded in sight of the other vessel, not in restricted visibility."* Without these signals, there is no way to coordinate intentions as the crossing or head-on rules assume.

3. **Rule 19 replaces the geometric encounter rules.** Because the specific encounter type is indeterminate, Rule 19 provides a **blanket directive** — avoid turning to port — that works as a universal safety default. If both vessels independently follow this same rule, turning to starboard (or stopping), the risk of turning *into* each other's path is minimized. A port turn, by contrast, could swing your vessel across the projected track of the other vessel in any of the possible encounter geometries, creating exactly the close-quarters situation you cannot see to resolve.

## In Summary

The conclusion that **port is least advisable** comes from Rule 19's restricted-visibility provision, not from the crossing give-way rule, precisely because **in fog you lack the visual information needed to classify the encounter** and lack the ability to exchange maneuvering signals — the two prerequisites on which the normal crossing, head-on, and overtaking rules depend.

> *"Unless you are overtaking, avoid if at all possible **altering your course to port**; whenever possible alter course to **starboard**."*

Therefore, **turning to port is the least advisable action**.

---

## Why the Crossing Give-Way Rule Cannot Resolve This Alone

This is the critical analytical point. The usual crossing rule (Rule 15, Page 1) states:

> *"The vessel which has the other on her **own starboard side** shall keep out of the way."*

This rule depends on **two prerequisites that cannot be satisfied in this scenario**:

### 1. Vessels Must Be **In Sight of One Another**
The crossing and overtaking rules (Rules 13–17) are explicitly **sight-of-vessel rules**. The quick reference notes:

> *"Short blast signals are only sounded **in sight of the other vessel, not in restricted visibility**."*

This same principle underlies the maneuvering rules — they presuppose **visual contact**, not radar detection alone.

### 2. The Contact's **Classification is Unknown**
To apply Rule 15, you must confirm:
- It is a **crossing** situation (not overtaking, not head-on)
- You have the other vessel on your **starboard side**

Since the vessel **cannot be clearly classified** and is only detected by radar, you cannot determine:
- Its aspect or heading
- Whether it is overtaking you (which would change your role entirely)
- Which side it will ultimately present

## The Governing Framework Shifts Entirely

| Condition | Governing Rule | Turning Guidance |
|---|---|---|
| In sight, crossing, other to starboard | Rule 15 | Give way — alter as needed |
| In sight, crossing, other to port | Rule 15/17 | Stand on |
| **Fog, radar contact forward of beam, unclassified** | **Rule 19** | **Starboard preferred; port least advisable** |

### Why Rule 19 Supersedes Here:
Rule 19 operates as a **standalone fog protocol** precisely because classification is unreliable in restricted visibility. It adopts a **conservative, asymmetric default** — favor starboard — which:

1. **Mirrors the head-on rule** (both vessels alter starboard → pass port-to-port)
2. **Avoids compounding error** if the other vessel is also altering (two vessels both turning starboard diverge; both turning port converge)
3. **Does not require knowing** the other vessel's classification or exact bearing

Turning **port is least advisable** because Rule 19 explicitly discourages it in fog regardless of the contact's apparent position. The crossing give-way rule *cannot substitute* because it requires visual confirmation of vessel status and relative geometry — conditions that fog and radar ambiguity specifically deny you. Rule 19 exists precisely to fill this gap with a simpler, safer default action.
